s1.method: I ran my own script (audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/UX-HOME-1/s1-ipad-glance.mjs) against the local rig in WebKit: Eli on the iPad in portrait and landscape, and Elizabeth in landscape for the timer pill. It reads each element's computed font size and converts it to cap height with SF Pro's 0.705 ratio rather than the investigator's canvas measurement, at 0.1924 mm/px. I also read the type tokens and overrides in apps/design.css and index.html.
s1.observed: Font sizes are the same in both orientations. Kicker 12 px is 1.63 mm. Greeting 44 px is 5.97 mm, the only item at or above 5.8 mm (H2 at 2 m). Summary line 14 px is 1.9 mm. F260 ring '2/5' 18 px is 2.44 mm. '.gbig' lines 22 px ('Acts 6', '3 to eat this week', '6 to pray') are 2.98 mm, or 5.1 arcmin at 2 m, which is right at the 20/20 limit. Fridge item names and days 12 px are 1.63 mm (2.8 arcmin, below even the 20/20 limit). Kids chip and reminders 18 px are 2.44 mm. Feed text 16 px is 2.17 mm. Timer pill '6:20' 16 px is 2.17 mm. The computed tokens on the iPad are --fs-xs 12, --fs-md 16, --fs-xl 22 with data-kind=adult. design.css overrides the type scale only for kid (:280-282) and kiosk (:286-287), and index.html has no width or iPad media query that raises type. H2 at 2 m needs 5.8/0.1924/0.705 = 42.8 px type and H1 needs 73.7 px, which matches the report's ~43 and ~74 px and its 2-4.6x factor.
s1.rationale: The claim holds and my numbers are within 0.1-0.2 mm of the report's. Nothing on adult Home except the greeting reads at 2 m, which misses the constitution's 2-3 m requirement (HUB-AUDIT-PROMPT.md:116-117). The rating is still inflated. Nothing is broken or wrong: every number reads fine at arm's length, and walking up to the iPad is an easy workaround. That fits the rule's medium ('a core daily flow is noticeably hampered though a workaround exists'), not high ('broken or wrong'). Exposure: every adult who glances at the 24/7 kitchen iPad from across the room, every day.
s1.correction: The headline range '2.3-3.1 mm' leaves out the smallest key information the constitution names, leftovers expiring. The fridge item names and 'Nd' days are 12 px, 1.6-1.7 mm, so the key-information range is about 1.6-3.1 mm. The rating should be medium, not high: a workaround exists (step up to the iPad) and no flow is broken.

s2.method: I wrote my own script that walks every visible text node in #view-home on the local rig (typical, demo clock, WebKit). For each node it measures the computed font size and the canvas cap height, then converts to mm at 25.4/132 mm per CSS px (iPad Air 11"). I ran it for Eli on the iPad in portrait and landscape, and for Ezra in portrait, then checked the type tokens in apps/design.css.
s2.observed: Adult Home has 131 text runs, identical in portrait and landscape. Font sizes are 12 px (41 runs), 14 (4), 16 (52), 16.6 (13), 18 (17), 22 (3) and 44 (1). The largest are the greeting at 44 px (5.97 mm cap), then "Acts 6", "3 to eat this week" and "6 to pray · 3 done" at 22 px (3.08 mm), then the "2/5" ring and the card titles at 18 px (2.5 mm). Only the greeting reaches H2 at 2 m (5.81 mm). Nothing reaches H1 at 2 m or H2 at 3 m. Kid Home: greeting 5.97 mm, star "3" 4.62 mm. Recomputed thresholds with a 0.705 cap ratio: H2 at 2 m needs about 42.7 px type and H1 about 73.7 px, so the 43/74 px and 2–4.6x figures hold. design.css:22-23 sets --fs-xl to 22px; only [data-kind=kid] (:280-283) and [data-kind=kiosk] (:285-288) rescale type. There is no width or iPad rule; the only @media rules there are grid layout (:345-346).
s2.rationale: The facts are right. But the rating 'high' needs a core daily flow to be broken, and it is not: every number on Home reads normally at arm's length, so the workaround is to step up to the iPad. The fairer reading is 'a core daily flow is noticeably hampered though a workaround exists', which is medium. The constitution names across-the-room reading of today's reading, timers and leftovers as a requirement for the 24/7 iPad (HUB-AUDIT-PROMPT.md:116-117), so this is not low: the 22 px key numbers (3.08 mm) sit right at the 20/20 acuity limit at 2 m (about 2.9 mm) and below it at 3 m (4.36 mm). Neither H1 nor H2 is a standard. So the across-the-room glance is noticeably hampered, but the flow is not broken.
s2.correction: Nothing is factually wrong. The 'high' rating is inflated: the glance is hampered, not broken (reading at arm's length works), so medium.

s1.method: I ran my own script (audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/UX-HOME-2/s1-tv-text.mjs) on the local rig: the kiosk profile at 1920x1080 in WebKit, computed font size x 0.705 cap ratio x mm/px for 43/55/65-inch 1080p panels, plus the board's geometry. I read the kiosk CSS in index.html:128-175 and design.css:286-287 and 417.
s1.observed: On a 55-inch TV at 3 m (H2 = 8.7 mm): the date kicker is 12 px, 5.4 mm, because the kiosk scale does not override --fs-xs and .hero-kicker uses it. Face labels, '★3' star counts, feed times and reminder bylines are all 18 px (--fs-sm), 8.0 mm, just 8% under H2 and about double the 20/20 limit (4.4 mm). What passes on 55 inches: clock 172.8 px (77 mm), verse refs 56 px (25 mm), greeting 40 px (17.9 mm), feed names and feed text 26 px (11.6 mm), and pane titles and reminder text 22 px (9.8 mm). On 43 inches the pane titles and reminder text also drop below H2 (7.7 mm), and the labels fall to 6.3 mm. On 65 inches everything except the kicker (6.3 mm) passes. Geometry: scrollHeight 1088 on a 1080 viewport, last pane bottom 1064, 4 reminders. That matches the height correction the item repeats.
s1.rationale: The measurements are right, but the harm is smaller than medium needs. The board's primary content passes H2 on a 55-inch panel: clock, verse refs, greeting, feed lines, reminders, and the 72 px avatars that identify who prayed or read. The failing text is secondary labels next to those. They miss the 20/40 threshold by 8% and stay readable to normal vision. Only the date kicker clearly fails, and the date is a secondary cue beside a 77 mm clock. The visual rule gives medium only for a real effect (misleads, hides information, measurably hampers reading), so this is low. Exposure: people with weaker eyesight (grandparents) reading the star counts and date from the couch; worse if the Downstairs TV is 43 inches, a size nobody has recorded. The reminder overflow (5-6 reminders, no '+N more') could hide information, but P2-VIS-02 owns it and I did not re-test it here.
s1.correction: The headline 'the board's news is its smallest text' is misleading. The feed's news lines themselves are 26 px (11.6 mm on 55 inches) and pass H2. The failures are the 12 px date kicker (5.4 mm) and 18 px secondary labels (face names, ★ counts, feed times, bylines) at 8.0 mm, which miss H2 by only about 8%. Medium overstates this: the rating should be low.

s2.method: I wrote my own script that measures every visible text node in #tv as the kiosk profile at 1920x1080 on the rig. It converts cap height to mm for 43/55/65" 16:9 panels and grades each one against H2 and H1 at 3 m and against the 20/20 limit (5 arcmin, 4.36 mm). It also records the board height and the bottom of the last pane. I viewed my screenshot and read the kiosk token block and the .tv CSS.
s2.observed: On a 55" panel at 3 m (H2 = 8.72 mm): the kicker (12 px, --fs-xs, not overridden in the kiosk block) is 5.7 mm. Face labels, the stars ★3/★1, feed times and reminder bylines (18 px) are 8.2 mm. All of these fail H2, but every one is above the 20/20 limit. The feed lines themselves ("Added a reminder…", 26 px) are 11.4 mm, and reminder text and pane titles are 10.1–11.4 mm; all pass H2. Avatars are 72 px (about 46 mm). On a 43" panel the 18 px items are 6.4 mm and reminder text is 7.9 mm (fails). On a 65" panel everything except the kicker passes. Board: scrollHeight 1080 and last pane bottom 1064 (the report says 1088), with 4 reminders and 5 feed rows.
s2.rationale: The TV is a primary device. On the claimed 55" panel the failures are 6% under a non-standard 20/40 heuristic, and still about 1.9 times the 20/20 limit. The only big miss is the date kicker, and the date is not key information on this board. Who prayed or read is also shown by 72 px avatars. That is cosmetic and does not measurably hamper reading, so it is low under the visual-item rule. The part that does hide information (reminders dropping off with no '+N more') is owned by the Visual section, so it is not rated here. Exposure: if the Downstairs TV is 43" or smaller, the 18 px labels and the 22 px reminders fall further short, but they still read to a normal eye at 3 m.
s2.correction: The title is misleading. The news itself (feed lines, 26 px, 11.4 mm at 55") passes H2 and is larger than the pane titles' siblings. The items that fail are metadata: the date kicker, name labels, ★ counts, times and bylines. The star count in the Stars pane (18 px) is smaller than its own heading (26 px). All the 55" failures except the kicker miss by only 6%. I measured the board at 1080 px, not 1088 (content still ends at y=1064).

s1.method: I ran my own script (audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/GAP-HOME-1/s1-timer-visibility.mjs) on the typical seed, where Elizabeth has a 15-minute timer with 6:20 left. It opened Home on the TV kiosk, the iPad as Eli, Ezra and Elizabeth, and Dad's iPhone, recorded the pill and any on-page mention of the timer, and queried /api/data/timer as mom and as eli. I read the timer code at index.html:773-830 and the TV board markup at :1117-1128.
s1.observed: Pill visible only for Elizabeth ('6:20', 16 px, 155x44 at y=744). TV kiosk, iPad as Eli, iPad as Ezra and Dad's iPhone: pill hidden, and no text on the page mentions the timer or the time left. The API returns timer.active only in mom's person scope. Eli's person-scope pull has just lastPreset 600, and the family timer scope is empty. The code reads hub.get('timer.active', {app:'timer', scope:'person'}) (index.html:780, 786, 814). The TV board markup (index.html:1119-1128) has no timer pane, and apps/timer.html is data-scope="person" with no hub.activity call, so the feed never mentions a running timer either. The pill's 16 px is 2.2 mm cap on the iPad.
s1.rationale: Confirmed as stated. The constitution names running timers as key information on the 24/7 iPad (HUB-AUDIT-PROMPT.md:116-117). The kitchen timer cannot be seen by anyone but the person who started it: not on the shared kitchen iPad when someone else is signed in, not on the TV, not on another adult's phone, and no feed line. A secondary household job, keeping an eye on a kitchen timer someone else set, cannot be done, which is the rule's medium for a gap. The switching case (P2-PROF-08, medium) and the pill size (UX-HOME-1) overlap and are owned elsewhere. The remaining gap is still medium, because a timer started on one device never reaches the shared iPad signed in as another person, even with no switch. Not tested here: whether an iPhone-started timer alerts at all when the PWA is backgrounded; the local rig cannot show that.

s2.method: I wrote my own script on the rig (typical seed, where Elizabeth/mom has timer.active with 6:20 left). It reads the timer rows through the API as mom, Eli and the TV, opens Home on the TV, then on the iPad as Eli, Ezra and mom (portrait and landscape), and records pill visibility, text and cap height and the TV pane titles. It then opens the Timer app as mom and measures the countdown. I read index.html:773-826 and the TV board markup.
s2.observed: Only mom's person scope has timer.active; Eli's has only lastPreset, and the kiosk's family timer rows are empty. The pill is hidden on the TV, on the iPad as Eli and on the iPad as Ezra. As mom it shows 6:20 at 16 px, 2.31 mm cap (portrait and landscape). The TV's panes are Verse / Prayed today / Stars / Around the house / Reading today / Reminders, with no timer. The shell reads hub.get('timer.active', {app:'timer', scope:'person'}) (index.html:780, 786) and renders only that (:814). The kiosk has a pill style (:355) and a comment saying the display profile 'only looks: pill' (:777), but it has no timer of its own, so it never shows one. With the Timer app open as mom, the countdown is 88 px (12.1 mm digit height), which passes H1 at 2 m.
s2.rationale: A kitchen timer shared across the household is a secondary job, and the missing capability means it cannot be done. When someone else signs in on the kitchen iPad, or someone looks at the TV, a running timer is invisible. The only workaround is switching back to the owner, which is clumsy. That matches medium ('a secondary job cannot be done, or needs a clumsy workaround'). It is not high because the owner still has a readable surface: keep the Timer app open (12.1 mm), so the cooking timer itself works. The silencing on switch is owned by P2-PROF-08, which I did not re-rate.
s2.correction: Nothing stated is wrong. The item leaves out that the owner already has a room-readable surface: the Timer app's own countdown is 88 px / 12.1 mm on the iPad (passes H1 at 2 m). The 'too small to read across the room' point applies to the Home pill only. It also leaves out that the kiosk pill styling and the 'display profile only looks' comment (index.html:355, 777) show the TV was meant to display a timer.

s1.method: I read the grid CSS at index.html:217-235 and wrote my own script (s1-measure.mjs, WebKit, local rig, typical data, Eli). It measured every tile, not only the first one, on iPhone PWA and Safari and on iPad portrait and landscape. I also looked at density-apps-iphone-pwa.png and compared the results with layout.json tiles.nonSquare.
s1.observed: iPhone 430: 4 columns. The small tiles are 91 px wide at a 103 px pitch. The icon plate is 48 px, the glyph 29 px and the label 12 px (--fs-xs). Leftovers, Timer and both Dollywood tiles have 2-line labels and measure 91x102; Prayer, Tally, Kid Verse and Verses stay 91x91 in the same rows, so row bottoms are ragged by 11 px. iPad portrait: 118x118 tiles in 6 columns, still with a 48 px icon. iPad landscape: 98x98 tiles in 8 columns, and the 2-line Dollywood tiles are 98x102. Every tile is at least 91 px, well above the 44 px minimum. The 12 px labels are dark ink (--text #2E251D) on the #FFFCF8 surface, far above WCAG AA. The kid grid is different: 88 px icons and 191-277 px tiles.
s1.rationale: This is a visual item. Under the rule, medium needs a real effect on use: it misleads, hides information, or measurably hampers reading or tapping on a primary device. None of that applies here. All targets are 2x the 44 px minimum, the labels are high-contrast 12 px (about iOS home-screen label size), and nothing is hidden. The non-square 2-line tiles (11 px taller) and the small icon inside large iPad tiles are cosmetic, so the rating is low.
s1.correction: Two details are off. First, 'a 29 px glyph, about half the size of an iOS icon' compares the glyph with a whole iOS icon. The comparable element is the 48 px icon plate, which is about 80% of a 60 pt iOS icon. Second, 'one size everywhere' holds only for adults, because the kid grid uses 88 px icons. The facts that hold are: only the 2-line tiles are 91x102, their 1-line neighbours stay 91x91 (ragged rows), and the iPad tiles go from 118 to 98 px in landscape. The medium rating is inflated because there is no reading or tapping harm.

s2.method: I read the grid CSS at index.html:216-240 and design.css:22 (--fs-xs), and checked the arithmetic: (398-3x12)/4 = 90.5 px tiles, and a 2-line tile is 2+16+48+8+2x12x1.15 = 101.6 px tall. I then measured every tile myself on the local rig (WebKit, typical data) on iphone-pwa, iphone-safari, ipad-portrait and ipad-landscape (s2-g02.mjs), and looked at density-apps-iphone-pwa.png and density-apps-ipad-landscape.png.
s2.observed: The icon is 48 px everywhere (index.html:226 has no media query), the glyph is 29 px and the label is 12 px on every device. Phone: 4 columns of 90.7 px tiles at about a 103 px pitch. 4 of the 8 small tiles are 90.6x101.7 because their labels wrap to 2 lines (Larder Ledger, Kitchen timer, the build guide, the park map). iPad portrait: all tiles are 118x118 and square, including the 2-line ones. iPad landscape: tiles are 98 px (the 896 px grid beside the 220 px sidebar, 8 columns); the build guide and park map tiles are 98.2x101.8. Every target is at least 90 px, twice the 44 px minimum. The labels use var(--text) on var(--surface), so contrast is not in question.
s2.rationale: All the facts are true, but this is cosmetic: the grid is uniform, the chrome looks large around a small glyph, 2-line tiles are about 11 px taller, and the iPad does not scale the icon up. Nothing misleads or hides information, targets are far above 44 px, and 12 px labels are about the size of iOS home-screen labels, with no AA failure. The rule says a visual item is medium only with a real effect on use (misleading, hiding information, or measurably hampering reading or tapping); otherwise it is low. So medium is inflated.
s2.correction: Rating inflated: low, not medium. The comparison of the 29 px glyph with 'an iOS icon' mixes a glyph with a whole icon; the 48 px icon well is about 80 % of a 60 pt iOS icon. The comment at index.html:217 is about column tracks not growing next to a wide tile. Non-square tiles occur on the phone (4 of 8) and in iPad landscape (2 of 8), not on iPad portrait.

s1.method: I ran my own measurement of Home for Eli on iPhone PWA and Safari and on iPad portrait and landscape (same s1-measure.mjs run; output copied to UX-HOME-3/s1). I recorded the card boxes, the Reminders and feed card boxes, the feed row count and the #views scrollHeight. I checked the result against density.json and home-typical-iphone-pwa-light.png, and read the .glance CSS at index.html:105-107.
s1.observed: iPhone PWA: 4 full-width cards of 398 px width and 246, 288, 214 and 196 px height. 2 of them sit fully above the 859 px visible bottom (1 in Safari at 667). The Reminders card spans 1222-1790 (list at 1295), and the feed card spans 1806-4319 with 30 rows (list at 1883). The page is 4415 px, which is 4.74 viewports of 932 or 5.1 of the visible 859 px. The feed card alone is 2513 px (57% of the page); everything above it ends at 1790 px, about 2.1 visible screens. iPad portrait: all 4 cards are visible, the Reminders card spans 760-1198 against a fold at 1107, and the page is 3243 px. iPad landscape: the Reminders card header starts at 742 and the list at 815, against a fold at 820. The feed runs beside it from 742, and the page is 3681 px.
s1.rationale: Every number is true, but the effect is one or two ordinary scrolls on the iPhone to reach the Reminders. Nothing is hidden, broken or misleading, and on the primary shared device (Kitchen iPad, portrait) all four cards and most of the Reminders are above the fold. That is a minor inconvenience, which is low. The medium bar, 'a core daily flow noticeably hampered', is not met, because scrolling a phone dashboard is the normal interaction.
s1.correction: The facts are right. Still, '4.7 screens tall' mostly measures the 30-row activity feed, a naturally long log at the bottom (2513 of 4415 px). The dashboard content above it is about 2 phone screens. The medium rating is inflated.

s2.method: I re-measured Home as Eli (typical data, WebKit) on iphone-pwa, iphone-safari, ipad-portrait and ipad-landscape with my own script. It records the #views scroll height, the tab-bar fold, the tops and heights of the card, Reminders and feed, and the number of feed lines. I checked the order of cards in index.html:1160-1203 and the one-column rule at :105-107.
s2.observed: iPhone PWA: the page is 4415 px, 4.74 viewports (5.14 of the 859 px area above the tab bar). The 4 cards are 398 px wide and 196-288 px tall (reading 226-472, fridge 484-772, prayer 784-998, kids 1010-1206), so 2 fit above the fold. The Reminders card heading is at 1222 and its list at 1295; the feed card starts at 1806 and is 2513 px (57 % of the page), 30 lines in 18 groups with Show more. Safari (740 px): the fold is at 667, 1 card fits, 5.97 viewports. iPad portrait: 3243 px, all 4 cards visible, Reminders list at 833. iPad landscape: 3681 px, the Reminders card and feed card both start at 742 side by side, the list starts at 815, the fold is at 820, and the feed card is 2907 px. The hero sub-line at the top already says 'a reading waiting · 3 to eat · 6 to pray · 4 reminders'.
s2.rationale: The numbers are right, but the harm is small. The daily glance (reading, fridge) is above the fold on the iPhone PWA. Prayer and Kids need one short scroll, and Reminders about 450 px of scrolling, with its count already shown in the hero. Most of the height is the 30-row activity feed at the bottom, which is naturally last and paged. On the Kitchen iPad in portrait all 4 cards show. This is a minor inconvenience, not a core daily flow noticeably hampered, so it is low rather than medium.
s2.correction: The 1295 'Reminders' figure is the list top; the card heading starts at 1222 (iPhone) and 742 (iPad landscape), so in landscape the Reminders heading is visible above the 820 fold and only its items fall below it. The page height is dominated by the feed card (2513 of 4415 px on iPhone), not by the four cards. Rating inflated: low, not medium.

s1.method: I read apps/verses.html:160-243 and the index.html data declarations. I searched index.html, worker/src/chat.js and worker/src/reminders.js for any reader of verses or summary. I extracted noHomePresence from ia.json and checked it against apps.json and the Home card code (index.html:680-705, 773-805, 902-918).
s1.observed: verses.html:172 documents summary as 'for the Home card (read by index.html...)', and writeSummary() at :239-243 writes {due, streak, boxes, total, reviewedToday, week, at}. index.html:458-459 declares reminders, f260, leftovers, prayer, hub, timer, dollywood-live and kidverse, with no verses. index.html contains no 'verses' string apart from a comment at :986, and no worker file reads it: no chat tool and no push. So the summary is a dead write, and a due verse review has no cue anywhere outside the app. ia.json has 6 adult and 6 kid noHomePresence entries, matching 9 and 7 visible apps. However, the Timer has a shell pill on every tab, Home included, while it runs (index.html:343-358, 404, 773-805). The adult Kids card also shows Kid Verse star data, but it has no open button.
s1.rationale: The missing capability is a glanceable 'N verses due' on Home. Verses opens in 2 taps (Apps, then tile) with about 80 ms first paint, and the app itself shows the due queue. That makes this a nice-to-have, not a job that cannot be done or needs a clumsy workaround, so it is low under the feature-gap rule. It does weaken the spaced-repetition habit, because nothing prompts a review, but Verses is a secondary app.
s1.correction: 'Timer has no Home presence' is only partly true. A running timer shows a pill on Home and on every tab, and the investigator's metric counted only cards and entry buttons. The adult Kids card also shows Kid Verse data, without a link. The code comment claiming index.html reads the summary is the real defect in wording. The medium rating is inflated: the job, reviewing due verses, can still be done in 2 taps.

s2.method: I read the comment and writeSummary() in apps/verses.html, the channel declarations at index.html:458-459 and the Home card builders, and grepped apps/, worker/src and index.html for any reader of verses.summary. On the local rig I opened Verses as Eli, returned to Home, and read the local cache, the server rows (/api/data/verses?scope=person via apiAs) and the Home card titles.
s2.observed: apps/verses.html:172-173 says the summary is 'for the Home card (read by index.html, never by this app)'. writeSummary() at :238-243 writes it, and the server holds it: {due:3, streak:13, boxes:[2,2,6,14,40], total:64, reviewedToday:0}. index.html declares no 'verses' channel at :458-459. The only 'verses' match in index.html is a comment at :986, and worker/src has no reader. After opening Verses, the Home cards are Today's reading, In the fridge, Prayer, Kids, Reminders and Around the house, with no mention of due verses. The adult noHomePresence list in ia.json has 6 entries, but the Timer app has a shell pill on Home while a timer runs (index.html:404, :813), and Kid Verse's data drives the adults' Kids card (kidStars at :885, used at :1196).
s2.rationale: The summary is written and never read, and the code comment is false. The missing capability is a 'N verses due' nudge on Home. Reviewing verses still works in 2 taps (Apps, then Verses), which then lists what is due, and memory-verse review is a secondary job, not a core one. So the gap is a nice-to-have (low), not a secondary job that cannot be done or needs a clumsy workaround (medium).
s2.correction: '6 of 9 apps have no Home presence' overstates it. The Timer shows as a pill on Home whenever one is running, and Kid Verse's stars feed the adults' Kids card, so strictly 4 of 9 (Tally, the build guide, the park map outside park days, Verses) have none. The dead-write finding itself is correct. Rating inflated: low, not medium.

s1.method: Read index.html:1146-1156 and 902-910 and the kid Home screenshots, then ran my own WebKit measurement of Ezra's Home on iphone-pwa, ipad-portrait and ipad-landscape. The script recorded every control, its size and whether it has an icon, the Reminders card's share of the page, and where the big CTA leads.
s1.observed: Kid Home has two controls. (1) 'Let's play — open your apps' is 398x117 px on iPhone and 788x106 on iPad portrait, with a 64 px sparkle icon tile; it does not open an app but switches to #apps, where all 7 tiles carry icons. (2) 'Open Kid Verse' (174x64, no icon) is the only data-open, one-tap launch into an app. No Prayer card or link on kid Home ('pray' does not appear in the view); Prayer is one of the 7 icon tiles on Apps. With 4 reminders the read-only Reminders card (0 done buttons for a kid) is 560 px tall on iPhone and 432 px on iPad. That is 48% (iPhone), 43% (iPad portrait) and 40% (iPad landscape) of Home's height, but only 29% of the iPhone viewport and 39% of the iPad-portrait viewport at rest. The icon-only Apps tab in the tab bar is always present.
s1.rationale: This is not a broken or noticeably hampered flow. A pre-reader can open any app, Prayer included, by icon and position alone: the big sparkle tile or the Apps tab icon, then an icon tile. That costs one extra tap versus the text-only 'Open Kid Verse'. The reminders are inert text taking up space. Under the rule (medium needs a secondary flow broken or misleading, or a core flow noticeably hampered), this is a minor inconvenience plus a constitution-style gap (HUB-AUDIT-PROMPT.md:118-119), so low.
s1.correction: 'The only one-tap entry is a text button' is true only for launching an app directly. The large CTA has a 64 px icon tile and leads in one tap to an all-icon Apps grid, so the kid flow is completable without reading. 'Reminders take up half of the screen' is about 40-48% of Home's page height with 4 reminders, and 29% (iPhone) / 39% (iPad portrait) of the viewport at rest.

s2.method: Read index.html:1146-1156 (the kid Home branch) and 902-910 (starsCardHtml), and viewed home-kid-typical-{ipad-portrait,ipad-landscape,iphone-pwa}-light.png. Ran audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/UX-HOME-7/s2-kid-home.mjs as Ezra on three devices. s1.method: Searched the park map and the Worker for any arrival, leave or geofence logic or local notification. Read parkJob and runCron in worker/src/reminders.js and the cron schedule in wrangler.toml. Checked whether anything calls rally(). No experiment was needed, because the code settles each claim.
s1.observed: apps/dollywood-live.html has no geofence, arrival or leave detection and no Notification call. onProperty/placeOf (:1170-1177) only label places in the pill and the Family pane. The only proximity-style push is parkJob (reminders.js:209-238): a kid's marker older than 30 min while an adult's is fresh. It runs only on the 8 am and 8 pm New York cron runs (reminders.js:252-255; wrangler.toml:25), which fits 'barely fires' (P2-PWA-02). rally() is defined at :1588 and nothing calls it, so the 'Meet at <name>' push cannot be sent (P2-PWA-18). The live map with 30 s redraws (:1484) and the Family pane's place and 'ago' per person (:1305) are the workaround.
s1.rationale: Gap rule: medium means 'a secondary job cannot be done, or needs a clumsy workaround'; low means 'nice to have'. Knowing that someone reached the meeting point, or where a kid is, can be done today by opening the map or the Family pane, which update live. The household's kids are pre-readers (heights 40-43 in) who are with an adult at the park, so an automatic 'left the park' alert is a convenience, not a missing daily job or a kid-safety hole in the shipped code. The genuinely broken pieces (the stale-kid timing, the rally push) are already rated under P2-PWA-02 and P2-PWA-18, and counting them here again would double-count them. So the rating is inflated by one step.
s1.correction: The claims are accurate. Only the rating is too high: medium should be low, since checking the live map or Family pane is a reasonable workaround and the related defects are filed and rated on their own.

s2.method: I searched apps/dollywood-live.html, apps/hub.js, index.html and worker/src for any arrival, leave, geofence or local-notification logic. I checked every call site of rally(), and read parkJob and runCron in worker/src/reminders.js against the cron triggers in worker/wrangler.toml to work out myself when the stale-kid push can run.
s2.observed: There is no geofence or arrival/leave logic anywhere. Every 'arriv*' hit in dollywood-live.html is about the viewer's own position ('In the arrival area') or direction steps. The page makes no showNotification or Notification call. rally() is defined at :1589 but never called: the only other match is the confirm() text 'Tap Rally afterwards…' at :1591. So POST /api/dollywood/rally, and with it the 'Meet at <name>' push, is unreachable from the UI (P2-PWA-18 holds). runCron (reminders.js:253-255) runs 'park' only when the New York hour is 8 or 20, even though the cron fires at four UTC hours. During a roughly 10 am-10 pm park day that means one check, at 8 pm. parkJob also only tests whether a kid's marker is more than 30 min old; it is not a proximity or arrival check. The only proximity cue is on screen: famPill (:1603-1604) shows the nearest family member and walking time, and the Family pane lists distances. Neither alerts anyone.
s2.rationale: Under the feature-gap rule, knowing that a family member has reached the meeting point or that a kid's phone has left the park is a secondary, park-day job. It can only be done clumsily, by repeatedly opening the map and watching markers, so this is medium ('a secondary job cannot be done, or needs a clumsy workaround'). It is not high: park days are occasional, not a core daily flow. The kid-safety angle (a leave alert for a kid's beacon) pushes toward the top of medium, and the kids' only automated safety net fires at most once in park hours. Exposure: every park day, for every adult watching a kid or waiting at a meeting point.

tie.method: I checked the point the two skeptics disagree on, which is whether the on-screen workaround is reasonable (low) or clumsy (medium). To do that I read how the park map keeps positions live: the geolocation watch, the visibilitychange handler and publish(). I also recomputed when the only push can run, from runCron/parkJob and the wrangler cron triggers, and checked every call site of rally(). The code settles the question, so I ran no experiment.
tie.observed: There is no arrival, leave or geofence logic and no local notification anywhere in apps/dollywood-live.html. rally() is defined at :1589 and nothing calls it, so the 'Meet at <name>' push cannot be sent. parkJob (reminders.js:209-238) only tests whether a kid's marker is more than 30 minutes old while an adult's is fresh. It is not a proximity check. runCron (:247-262) runs it only when the New York hour is 8 or 20, even though the cron fires at four UTC hours (wrangler.toml:25), so it gets at most one check during park hours, at 8 pm. Neither skeptic weighed one fact: the visibilitychange handler at :1475 calls clearWatch whenever the page is hidden, and publish() (:1250) only sends a live GPS fix. So a person's marker, a kid's beacon included, updates only while that person's phone has the map open in the foreground. The workaround s1 relies on (open the map or the Family pane and watch, :1484 30 s redraw, :1305) therefore works only if the other person is also keeping the map open on screen. Once their screen locks, their marker freezes and nothing tells the watcher, apart from the 'ago' text ageing and the once-at-8-pm stale push.
tie.rationale: This follows the feature-gap rule: medium is 'a secondary job cannot be done, or needs a clumsy workaround'. Knowing on a park day that someone has reached the meeting point, or that a kid's beacon has left or gone quiet, is a secondary job. Park days are occasional, so it is not a core daily flow, and high does not fit. The household clearly wants this job done: it built kid beacons, the rally push and the stale-kid push for exactly this. Inside the hub the job either cannot be done at all (leave alerts) or only by both people keeping the map in the foreground and one of them watching it. That is a clumsy workaround, not 'nice to have', so s1's low understates it. s1's double-counting argument does not hold. Even with P2-PWA-18 (rally) and P2-PWA-02 (cron timing) fixed, there would still be no arrival or leave alert. The gap is the missing capability, and the gap entry only cites those bugs as context. Exposure: every park day, for every adult coordinating with another adult or keeping track of a kid whose beacon is on.

s1.method: I read apps/dollywood.html (step card, boot and sheet code) and index.html:458-459 and renderHome. On the iPhone, Mark done is only reachable after the sheet is raised to half (at half it sits at 843-887 in 884). Home (Eli, iPad) opens only f260, leftovers and prayer, with no build-guide card. The missing Home card is a nice-to-have that Tally and Timer also lack. Under audits/02-shell.md:25-37 that is 'low: a minor inconvenience', not 'a core daily flow noticeably hampered'.

s1.method: Read the bootstrap in apps/dollywood.html:1061-1112: doneMap starts from legacy localStorage, and hub.get('progress') returns empty until the first pull. save() writes the whole map as one 'progress' row. Ran my own script on the local rig with four arms: an unheld first open polled every 25 ms; a warm-cache reopen with the pull held; a fresh iPhone with the pull held 5 s; and a fresh iPad that taps Mark done (JS click) inside the held window.
s1.observed: Fresh iPhone with the pull held: '0 of 9 done', Entrance chip 0/9, Mark done enabled, no loading words on screen, hub.sync.state 'offline' with lastPull null. After the pull: '7 of 9 done'. Tick during the window: server went from 24 ticks to 1, and the app then shows '1 of 9 done'. Control 1, warm cache with a held pull: correct '7 of 9 done' at once, so only a device with no cached copy is exposed. Control 2, unheld first open on the local rig: already '7 of 9 done' at the first 79 ms sample. The real window is therefore one network round trip on a fresh device (longer on slow or offline networks). The 5 s is an artificial hold. On the phone at peek, Mark done is below the sheet fold but enabled.
s1.rationale: The misleading state is 'a secondary flow is broken or misleading' = medium. It shows a first-time user's empty progress and leaves the one control that destroys the saved map enabled. The trigger is narrow: the first open on a new device or after storage is cleared, and a round-trip-length window on a normal network. A narrow trigger does not lower the rating, and the consequence of acting on the display is the loss of 23 of 24 ticks. That loss is rated separately under P2-SYNC-01, so I keep medium rather than raising it. The build guide is not a core daily household flow, so it is not high.

s2.method: Read the boot path in apps/dollywood.html and hub.ready in apps/hub.js. In my script I opened the guide on a fresh iPhone PWA with the person-scope pull held 5 s and 9 s, then ticked during a 9 s hold. As a control, I reopened on a device that already had a cache, again with the pull held.
s2.observed: Pull held 5 s, at 1.2 s: '0 of 9 done', chip 'Entrance & Plaza 94 ft · 0/9', Mark done enabled, no loading, syncing or wait wording, hub.sync 'offline'. After the pull: '7 of 9 done'. The 9 s hold gave the same picture. hub.ready caps its wait at 6 s (hub.js:334), yet the guide paints from an empty doneMap before ready resolves (dollywood.html:1061, :1105). A Mark done at 1.5 s in the 9 s window took the server from 24 ticks to 1. Control: a second open with the cache hub.cache.dollywood.person.eli showed '7 of 9 done' at once, so the blank window only occurs when that person has no cache on that device.
s2.rationale: The first-open screen misleads: it presents a returning builder as a first-time user and invites a tick that erases the saved progress. That tick's data loss is counted under P2-SYNC-01. The UX harm alone fits the medium rule line: 'a secondary flow is broken or misleading'. Exposure: only the first open per person per device (or after the cache is cleared), and only for as long as the first pull takes. That is usually under a second on home Wi-Fi, longer on a slow link. A narrow trigger does not lower the rating, and the consequence is severe, so medium stands; it is not high because the build guide is a secondary app.

s1.method: On the iPhone PWA (rig, WebKit) I made an online tick as a control, then went offline and tapped Mark done. I captured the app text, the shell's #syncdot state and position, whether the viewer covers the dot, and any toast. I then tested what that invisible pending state hides: while the phone was offline, a desktop signed in as Eli ticked another step, and then the phone reconnected. I ran this with the real clock and with the demo clock. Code: index.html:326 (viewer inset 0, z-index 30), 399 and 769 (the dot on the Me tab), apps/dollywood.html:1062.
s1.observed: Offline tick: '8 of 9 done', hub.sync {state:'offline', pending:1}. The page has no offline, pending, queued or sync wording and no toast. The viewer top bar reads only 'Hub | Dollywood build guide'. The online control looks identical: same count change, no wording, no toast. #syncdot does switch to 'dot dot-offline' at (383,876), but the full-screen viewer (0,0,430x932, z-index 30) covers it. Solo reconnect reaches 25 ticks, as the report says. With a concurrent tick on another device under the real clock, the server kept the desktop's show-14 and dropped the phone's offline entrance-08. The phone then silently reverted to '7 of 9 done'. The demo clock reversed which tick won because its slowed server clock skews the timestamps, so I rely on the real-clock run.
s1.rationale: This is 'a secondary flow is ... misleading' = medium. An offline tick is indistinguishable from a synced one, the one platform cue is hidden behind the viewer, and the person gets no warning. If they also tick on another device before this one reconnects, the tick they saw land vanishes without notice (the single-row LWW mechanism of P2-SYNC-01, which I do not count here). Offline use of the build guide is uncommon and a solo reconnect does flush, so it is not high.
s1.correction: The facts are right. For context: the hidden sync dot comes from the shell viewer covering the tab bar for every app, not from anything specific to Dollywood. 'On reconnect the server reached 25' holds only when nothing else changed meanwhile. With a concurrent tick on another device, the offline tick is dropped on reconnect under the real clock.

s2.method: On an iPhone PWA and an iPad portrait device, I opened the guide online, went offline through the rig and tapped Mark done. I then read the frame text, the shell text and toast, and used elementFromPoint to see what covers the shell's #syncdot. Finally I reconnected and read the server.
s2.observed: On both devices the count went from '7 of 9 done' to '8 of 9 done' while hub.sync was {state:'offline', pending:1}. Neither the frame nor the shell showed any offline, pending, queued or sync wording, and there was no toast. The shell's #syncdot has class 'dot dot-offline', but elementFromPoint at its centre (phone 383,876; iPad 633,1124) returns the app iframe inside #viewer (position:fixed, inset 0, z-index 30), so the dot is covered. The server stayed at 24 while offline and reached 25 after reconnecting. The guide has no sync wording of its own; only the live park map's family pane has one (apps/dollywood.html:1428).
s2.rationale: The claim is true, but the harm is small. The offline tick is not lost: it is queued in localStorage and syncs on reconnect, and I saw 25 on the server. The missing cue only matters when the person also ticks on a second device before the first one reconnects, and that danger is the whole-row overwrite already filed as P2-SYNC-01. The build guide is a home planning reference, so offline use is uncommon. This is a minor inconvenience with no misleading outcome in the usual case, so it is low under 'low: cosmetic, an edge case, or a minor inconvenience'. Medium would need a secondary flow that is actually broken or misleading in effect.
s2.correction: The facts are right, but the rating is inflated: medium to low. The report does not mention that the offline tick reliably reaches the server on reconnect (it cites 25 without drawing the conclusion), nor that the only real risk is the multi-device overwrite already filed as P2-SYNC-01.

tie.method: The two skeptics agree on every fact and differ only on severity, so I ran nothing new. I read both skeptics' outputs and checked the point in dispute against the code: how the guide saves progress, the scope it is stored in, how hub.js handles offline, and how the shell viewer covers the sync dot. I then applied the severity rule to the harm this item causes by itself, separate from P2-SYNC-01.
tie.observed: Both runs match the report. An offline tick moves the count to '8 of 9 done' with hub.sync {state:'offline', pending:1}. There are no offline, pending or sync words and no toast. The #syncdot 'dot dot-offline' sits at (383,876) on the phone and (633,1124) on the iPad, under #viewer (position fixed, inset 0, z-index 30, index.html:326). Once the device is back online on its own, the server goes 24 to 25 in both runs, so the tick is kept. The guide saves the whole map with hub.set('progress', …) (apps/dollywood.html:1062). Its scope is person, per apps.json:9 and data-scope="person" at apps/dollywood.html:684. So a tick is lost only when the same adult ticks on a second device of their own before the offline one reconnects. s1 saw exactly that under the real clock: the other device's show-14 was kept, the phone's entrance-08 was dropped, and the phone went back to '7 of 9 done'. That loss is the whole-row last-write-wins problem already filed as critical P2-SYNC-01 (audits/02-shell.md:63,129), which also happens online from a stale copy. hub.js does track the offline state (lines 240, 335, 340-341), but the only place it shows is the covered shell dot, and that is true for every app in the viewer, not just this one.
tie.rationale: Medium requires 'a secondary flow is broken or misleading'. The build-guide flow is not broken, because the offline tick is saved and syncs when the device reconnects. The count it shows is also true for that person's own progress. It is misleading only about whether the tick has synced yet. That becomes harmful only if the same person ticks on a second device before reconnecting, and the resulting loss is P2-SYNC-01, which is filed and rated separately, so it cannot count here. The harm left for this item is a missing 'not yet synced' cue in an uncommon offline use of a home planning guide. That fits 'low: cosmetic, an edge case, or a minor inconvenience'. s2's low holds; s1's medium relies on a loss that belongs to P2-SYNC-01, which s1 itself says it does not count.
tie.correction: The facts are right. The rating is too high: it should be low, not medium. The report does not say that the offline tick reliably reaches the server on reconnect (its own evidence shows 25). The only real loss, a tick on the same person's second device before reconnect, is P2-SYNC-01, not this item. The hidden sync dot is a shell problem that affects every app in the viewer (index.html:326, 399), not something specific to Dollywood.

s1.method: I opened the build guide inside the hub on the iPad (portrait, WebKit, as Eli, typical seed). I switched each of the five palettes with hub.setTheme. For every .bitem.ok I took the computed colour, multiplied the element's and its ancestors' opacity, composited the colour over the ancestor background chain and computed the WCAG ratio myself, without lib-vis. I checked the tokens against design.css and looked at the rendered step list.
s1.observed: 7 completed rows per palette: bold 13 px, line-through, opacity 0.55. Composited ratios are Hearth 2.23 (#75675B on rgb 255,252,248), Parchment 2.31, Frost 2.26, Midnight 3.62 and Forest 3.49, exactly the reported numbers. Without the 0.55 opacity the same text would be 5.34, 5.66, 5.46, 8.77 and 8.32, so the opacity alone causes the failure. The next open step reads at 5.34 in Hearth. The screenshot shows faint grey struck-through titles that are still readable up close, but with effort.
s1.rationale: Per the rule, medium covers text below WCAG AA on a primary device. This text is on the iPad and is less than half the 4.5 threshold in the light palettes, and the strike-through makes it harder to read still. Completed rows are still active controls: you tap one to revisit a step, so WCAG's exemption for inactive components does not apply. The exposure is modest: this is an adults-only hobby app, and the rows are deliberately played down while the ✓ still shows their status. That is why this sits at the bottom of medium, not higher.

s2.method: I recomputed the WCAG ratio from the tokens (--dim at opacity .55 over the card background). I then wrote s2-contrast.mjs, which opens the build guide inside the hub viewer (not standalone as Phase 3 did) on an iPad portrait in Hearth and Midnight and an iPhone. It reads the computed colour, the combined opacity and the nearest opaque background of the first .bitem.ok row, and screenshots #b-list.
s2.observed: Ticked rows are 13 px, weight 700, line-through, colour rgb(117,103,91) (Hearth) or rgb(201,187,171) (Midnight), with combined opacity 0.55, on the .build card background rgb(255,252,248) (Hearth) or rgb(36,30,25) (Midnight). Blended contrast measured in the hub viewer: Hearth 2.23:1 and Midnight 3.62:1, the same as the report. My hand calculation gives 2.16 to 2.25 in Hearth depending on the background, and 3.75 in Midnight against the page background. 7 of the 9 Entrance rows are ticked in the typical seed. For comparison, the current row is 12.25:1 (Hearth) and 16.14:1 (Midnight), and an unticked row is 5.34:1 (Hearth). Bold 13 px is not large text, so the AA bar is 4.5:1. In the screenshots the rows can be read, but they are faint.
s2.rationale: The rule gives text below WCAG AA on a primary device as an example of medium. These rows are also role=button tap targets for jumping back to a step, so the person has to read them to choose one, and to untick a step. Nothing exempts them, because a ticked row is still active and tappable. Medium is at the bottom of its range, though: the current step, which carries the main daily flow, is at 12:1, and the faded rows stay readable in bold.
s2.correction: 'Barely legible' overstates it. At 2.2:1 in bold the rows are faint but readable in both the iPad capture and my own. The Midnight figure depends on which background is used (3.62 against the card, about 3.75 against the page).

s1.method: I read setMode and init3D (apps/dollywood.html:1152-1270) and the step handlers (1084-1088). Then I ran my own experiment inside the hub on the iPad (WebKit, which created the WebGL canvas): open 3D, press Next, press Show on map, and record mode, which views are displayed and the step at each point.
s1.observed: init3D never reads curSec, curIdx, stepTarget or highlight. setMode('3d') sets the 2D svg and stage to display:none, and G.hl, which carries the step highlight, lives only in that svg. In the experiment, 3D mode showed step 8 of 9 with the svg hidden. Pressing Next moved to step 9 and immediately switched back to 2D, because stepNav → go() calls setMode('2d') (line 1087). Previous, Mark done and Show on map all go through go() too. So any step action leaves 3D and shows the step outlined on the 2D map.
s1.rationale: By the gap rule, medium means a secondary job cannot be done or needs a clumsy workaround, and low means nice to have. The job of locating and seeing the current step is done: every step action automatically fits the 2D map to the step's target with its highlight, which is one tap or no taps. What is missing is the step inside the 3D model. For a terrain-and-building guide that is added context, not the instruction itself, unlike LEGO Builder, where the 3D step is the instruction. The report's comparison therefore overstates it. The exposure is one adults-only hobby app, so the rating is low.
s1.correction: The code claim is correct. The report misses that Previous, Next, Mark done and Show on map all force the view back to 2D (apps/dollywood.html:1085-1087). The 2D map is therefore the app's designated view for a step, and the 3D view is not simply a place where the step is missing. The medium rating is inflated: the current step is always one action away with its highlight on the 2D map.

s2.method: I read setMode and init3D in apps/dollywood.html and searched every interaction with the 3D view (three., mode==='3d') across the whole 2,796-line file, not only lines 1157-1290. I then ran s2-3d-step.mjs on an iPad portrait inside the hub viewer: enter 3D, record what is visible and screenshot it, then use Next, a step-list row and Show on map while in 3D and record the mode.
s2.observed: The 3D code never reads curSec or curIdx. The camera starts from a fixed home position (cam.position HX+140,540,HZ+1300; target HX,40,HZ) and has no step focus. The only three.* calls from outside are resize, key and retexture. In 3D the 2D svg#map is display:none, so the #hl step highlight has zero size (hlVisibleInLayout false), and the screenshot shows a whole-park 3D view with no marker for the current step ('Planting, banners and signage'). Also, go() (line 1087), which Next, Previous, Mark done, Next unfinished, step-list rows and Show on map all call, runs setMode('2d') when in 3D. My run confirmed that each of those actions takes the view back to 2D and shows the highlight there. So the step flow and the 3D view cannot be used together.
s2.rationale: The claim is true as stated. On harm (the feature-gap rule): the core job of this app, finding where and what a build step is and ticking it off, is fully served by the 2D map highlight, the elevation line in the step text and the cross-section tool. The app deliberately sends every step action to 2D. Seeing the step in 3D is a nice-to-have for terrain steps, and the person can orbit the 3D model by hand. That is 'low = nice to have', not 'a secondary job cannot be done'. Exposure is adults on the iPad or desktop who use the 3D view while following steps.
s2.correction: The rating is inflated. The LEGO Builder comparison does not fit: in LEGO Builder the 3D model is the instruction, whereas here the steps are text plus a 2D highlight for a build done in another game (Planet Coaster 2), and the 3D view is a terrain reference. The report also misses a related fact: any step action taken in 3D (Next, Previous, Mark done, row tap, Show on map) switches the view back to 2D (line 1087). That makes the two modes deliberately separate rather than simply unconnected.

s1.method: I wrote my own WebKit script with a different method from the Phase 3 screenshot sweep. It resolves each target's computed colour, multiplies in the ancestor opacity, composites it over the nearest opaque background and computes the WCAG ratio, in all five palettes on a 430 px iPhone (typical plan, week 38). I then removed the body.nt New Testament tint to get Old Testament weeks, and cross-checked a few ratios by hand from the design.css tokens.
s1.observed: The key numbers match the report exactly. Past-week spans at opacity .6: 2.25 Hearth, 2.29 Parchment, 2.26 Frost, 2.88 Midnight, 2.82 Forest, so they fail in every palette. Past week numbers: 3.83 Hearth, 3.33 Parchment, 3.89 Frost; they pass in the dark palettes (5.88 and 5.58). The gold #chCount (21px/700, large text, 3:1 needed): 2.71 Hearth, 2.97 Parchment, 3.18 Frost, so it fails in Hearth and Parchment and passes in Frost. The 'This week' and 'MV' gold-on-gold-soft pills: 2.78, 3.11 and 3.30. The 'Today' kicker: 3.78, 4.04 and 4.15. Hearth muted captions are 4.49 on week 38. Two readings passed under my method. Unearned milestones read 5.92, because my method stops at the .mile's own background and ignores its opacity .55; worked by hand with that opacity they come to about 2.24, which matches the report's 2.1-2.4. The Journal tab reads 5.17 and 5.59; my method ignores the glass sheen gradient, so it cannot confirm or refute the report's sampled p10 of 4.39, 4.05 and 3.81. The core daily items pass: the Today title at 13.6 and Done at exactly 4.50 in Hearth. Unread cell vs page: 1.10 Hearth light, 1.14 Parchment, 1.09 Frost, 1.04 Midnight, Forest and Hearth-on-dark-OS; 1.05 Midnight and 1.09 Hearth on the NT-tinted week-38 page. The report's 1.04 and 1.10 are confirmed. Grid cells are 26x20 px. The filled olive state carries the progress at 3.7-4.3:1 in light and 8-9:1 in dark. In dark, the empty plan's grid, heatmap and book bar read as nearly blank. In the typical plan the grid looks like 3 rows plus a faint 4th, and the book bar seems to stop after Acts. In Hearth light the empty cells are still visibly discernible in the screenshot. Every count is repeated in text next to the graphics: '187 of 260 readings', '72% complete', '33 of 51 books finished', '52 weeks · tap one to open it'.
s1.rationale: Under the rule, a visual item is medium only if it misleads, hides information or measurably hampers use on a primary device. Here the information the graphics carry, which parts are done, is drawn in olive at well above 3:1. What is lost is the outline of the remaining or empty cells, mostly in the dark palettes. That information is duplicated in adjacent text, and tapping an unread future week is a secondary navigation. Cosmetic, with a real but minor legibility cost, so low (rule line: 'otherwise low').
s1.correction: The measurements and the dark-mode description are accurate. The medium rating is inflated: nothing is hidden that the adjacent text does not state, the done state stays well above 3:1, and in light palettes (1.09-1.14) the empty cells are still visible on screen.

s1.method: I read nextReading, renderToday, the hero code and every path that changes the current week. I then ran my own WebKit script on the typical household: remove 30-2, open F260 on an iPhone, record the Today card, hero, pace, the f260.summary row and every cue for week 30, then press Done until 30-2 is offered. A second run from a fresh reset taps the week stepper '+' once, to see how a gap arises.
s1.observed: With 30-2 unticked at week 38, both the Today card and the hero offer 'Acts 6 / Week 38 · Day 3'. Pace says 'On pace', and the Home summary row's next is 38-3; no text anywhere names week 30. 30-2 came up after exactly 73 Done taps, as 'Malachi 2 · Week 30 · Day 3 … · catching up' (73 = the rest of week 38 + weeks 39-52). At that moment the hero read 'Week 52 done / Plan complete 🎉' while 30-2 was still unread. Visual cues do exist: the grid cell (class part, 26x20, 'Week 30, 4 of 5'); the Week 30 header in the weeks list, undimmed (opacity 1 among .6 neighbours) with a 4-of-5 ring, at y 3,553 of a 5,772 px page; and a partly filled Malachi book-bar segment ('Malachi · 75%'). Exposure is real: one tap on the week stepper '+' (or the week select) moves the plan from 38 to 39 without asking, which buries 38-3 to 38-5 behind 70 later readings in the same way.
s1.rationale: F260 reading is a core daily flow for the adults, and this is its secondary job of catching up. The missed reading is not lost: it can be found and ticked through the grid or the weeks list. But the app never names it for about 14 weeks, and the only route is spotting a subtle undimmed header or a half cell. That fits medium ('a secondary job … needs a clumsy workaround'). It is not high, because the daily Done flow still works.
s1.correction: The report says 'The only cue before that is a half-filled 26×20 grid cell'. That is not accurate: the weeks list also shows Week 30 undimmed among dimmed finished weeks with a 4-of-5 ring, and the Malachi book-bar segment is partly filled. All of these cues are passive and far down the page. The report also misses a stronger symptom: when the 73 later readings are done, the hero reads 'Plan complete 🎉' while 30-2 is still unread; the Today card alone says 'catching up'.

s2.method: Read nextReading() and how the current week advances (setCurrent callers). Replayed the app's own PLAN and nextReading text in Node (s2-nextreading.mjs): weeks 1-37 read except 30-2, week 38 days 1-2 read, curWeek 38, then ticked whatever it offered until 30-2 came up. Checked what cues the week list gives for a partial past week.
s2.observed: The first reading offered is 38-2 'Acts 6'. 30-2 'Malachi 2' comes up only after 73 more ticks (3 left in week 38 plus 14 weeks of 5), which matches the report. Once offered it carries the '· catching up' label (f260.html:1565). A gap can be left behind only by moving forward by hand: the week picker (+ / select), or ticking a later week's reading, which calls setCurrent (f260.html:1592, 1707-1711). The Today card always offers the first gap in the current week, so someone following Today never leaves one. There are more cues than the grid cell. In the Plan week list, week 30's header stays at full opacity while the complete weeks around it are dimmed to .6 (f260.html:235), and it shows a '4' progress ring instead of a check (f260.html:252-256, 1306-1311). The half-filled grid cell is also a one-tap jump to week 30 (f260.html:1704). The missed reading is never lost: the plan cannot finish without it.
s2.rationale: The capability that is missing is proactively surfacing one specific missed reading. The reading can still be done with one or two taps once noticed (the grid cell or the week-30 row), and it comes up automatically at the end. Neither the core daily flow ('read today's reading, tap Done') nor any data is affected. Under the gap rule this is a nice-to-have with a simple workaround and a narrow trigger (moving forward by hand past an unticked day), so low rather than medium, which requires a secondary job that cannot be done or needs a clumsy workaround.
s2.correction: 'The only cue before that is a half-filled 26×20 grid cell' is wrong. The Plan week list also marks week 30: its header is not dimmed among the dimmed complete weeks and it shows a 4-of-5 ring, and the grid cell itself is a tap target that opens week 30. The report also does not say that the gap can only arise from moving forward by hand, never from following the Today card. The 73-readings figure is correct.

tie.method: The skeptics disagreed only on severity, so I checked how a gap arises and how visible it is. I read nextReading, the hero, the Today card, setCurrent and every caller, the week stepper markup, and the plan's row-tap handler. I then replayed the app's own PLAN and nextReading in Node (tb-replay.mjs) for three cases: the report's 30-2 gap, one tap on the stepper '+' at week 38, and a past day unticked by accident.
tie.observed: Case A (30-2 missing, plan at week 38): the first reading offered is 38-2 'Acts 6', and 30-2 'Malachi 2' comes up only after 73 more readings. That matches the report and both skeptics. Case B (one '+' tap at week 38, with 38-2 to 38-4 unread): 'Acts 10-11' (39-0) is offered first, and 38-2 only after 70 readings. The '+' button calls setCurrent(curWeek+1) with no confirm, and it sits next to 'Jump to current week' in the Plan tools row (f260.html:614-620, 1708). Case C (12-2 unticked by accident): 73 readings pass before it comes back. A tap anywhere on a [data-day] row in any week flips done[id] with no confirm (f260.html:1656-1660). Undo covers only Today's own Done (f260.html:1597-1600), so a stray tap on an old week's row makes a gap the reader may not see. Following Today alone never makes a gap: Today and the hero always offer the first gap in the current week first, and 'Start week N+1' shows only once the week is complete (f260.html:1340). Cues while the gap exists: the grid cell ('part', 26x20). Week 30's header stays undimmed with a 4-of-5 ring among dimmed weeks, at y 3,553 of a 5,772 px page. The Malachi bar reads 75%. Pace reads 'On pace', and the Home summary's next is 38-3 (s1-gap.json). When week 52 is done with the gap still open, the hero says 'Week 52 done / Plan complete 🎉' while Today says 'catching up' (f260.html:1560-1562, s1-gap.json ui30).
tie.rationale: The gap rule rates medium when 'a secondary job cannot be done, or needs a clumsy workaround'. Catching up a missed reading is a secondary job of the adults' daily F260 flow. Once the reader knows about the gap, fixing it takes two taps. But nothing tells them about it: Today, the hero, pace and the Home card all point elsewhere or read 'On pace', and at the end the hero even claims the plan is complete. The only route is spotting a passive cue: an undimmed header or a partly filled small cell far down a long page. That is a clumsy workaround, and the display misleads. s2's argument for low rests mainly on the narrow trigger, and the severity rule says a narrow trigger does not by itself lower a rating. The exposure is also wider than s2 states: one tap on the stepper '+' or one stray tap on a past day row makes a gap, with no confirm and no undo. It is not high: no data is lost, the daily Done flow works, and the reading does come back ('catching up') before the plan can really finish.
tie.correction: Two things in the report are wrong. First, it says 'The only cue before that is a half-filled 26×20 grid cell'. In fact the plan's week list also keeps Week 30's header undimmed with a 4-of-5 ring, and the Malachi book bar reads 75%. The grid cell is also a tap target that jumps to week 30. All of these cues are passive and far down the page. Second, the report leaves out how a gap arises and one symptom. A gap arises only from moving the plan week forward by hand (the stepper '+' or the week select, no confirm) or from unticking a past day (a row tap, no confirm or undo), never from following Today alone. When week 52 is done while a gap remains, the hero reads 'Plan complete 🎉'. The 73-reading figure is correct.

s1.method: I read apps/kidverse.html in full around the speech, award, reconcile and story code. s1.observed: Both speaker buttons read exactly 'Read it to me' (#say and #story-say, on every device). The story thumbnail is the same week art as the verse scene, so position is the only thing that tells the two apart. 'I heard it' has a check icon, and its instruction lives only in #story-sub text: 'Tap “I heard it” after someone reads it to you' (:665). Every piece of feedback goes through hub.toast only, and nothing calls speechSynthesis: :301/:312 cannot read aloud, :328 star already, :480 badge (with confetti), :484 cash-in/'Your week starts over.', :636 story already, :641 'Great listening!'. The spoken verse text (:303) and story text (:621) end without a next step such as 'now tap the star'. Nothing gates Done or 'I heard it' on having listened. ledger-rules.json L4 shows the reset case {done:'Done today ★', starCount:'0'}. The page re-renders only on hub.onChange (:519, :676), with no midnight timer. So 'past midnight' leaves yesterday's pressed button beside yesterday's count; it does not read 0. The kid's two daily jobs (verse ★, story heard) can be completed without reading, because each has a distinct icon in a fixed position. What needs reading is feedback: repeat-tap toasts, the badge toast (confetti carries the moment anyway), and parent-driven cash-in/reset toasts. The 'cannot read aloud' toast only appears where speech is missing, and iOS has speech. The two most harmful sub-points are already filed on their own. Done off the first screen is UX-KIDVERSE-2. 'Done today ★' beside 0 after a reset is UX-KIDVERSE-4, rated low. What is left is a minor inconvenience for pre-readers, so low.

s1.correction: "Loses logged by" is true only when someone other than the original logger fixes the item; the same person re-logging keeps their own name. The report leaves out two things. The ✓-and-re-log fix also posts a false "Finished the <item>" line to the family feed, which strengthens the item. I also read go() and the save handler to see whether the nav's own Add tab clears the form.
s1.observed: The button starts completely hidden (0 px visible above the nav) on four devices. iPhone PWA: save 846-904, nav top 807, frame height 884. iPhone Safari: save 846-904, nav 615, frame 692 (the report does not mention this device). iPad landscape: save 848-906, nav 695, frame 772. Desktop: save 843-900, nav 775. The + button path gives the same result (iPhone PWA 852-910). A tap aimed at the top of the button lands on the nav. On iPad portrait the button is fully clear (848-906 against a nav at 1055). Scrolling to the end always clears it: the page scrolls 172 px on iPhone PWA, 364 px on iPhone Safari, 286 px on iPad landscape and 200 px on desktop, and then the button sits above the nav (for example 674-732 against 807). go('add') only calls scrollTo(0,0) and does not clear the fields (apps/prayer.html:1153-1163), so tapping the highlighted nav 'Add' tab loses nothing.
s1.rationale: The claim is accurate, but the harm is a below-the-fold submit button on a 7-field form. One ordinary scroll of 170-360 px fixes it, and nothing is lost or misleading. Adding a request is an occasional task, not a core daily one. That fits 'low: cosmetic, an edge case, or a minor inconvenience' rather than 'medium: a secondary flow is broken or misleading, or a core daily flow is noticeably hampered'.
s1.correction: The facts are correct. The item also applies to iPhone Safari (save at 846 against a nav at 615) and to the + button path. The rating is inflated: medium should be low, because a single scroll reveals the button and the flow is occasional.

s1.method: I ran s1-kid-states.mjs on iPad portrait as Ezra and as Kiara, in light and dark. It reads each card's rendered fill, label, icon and title colour, taps an undone card twice, and computes the luminance ratio plus CIE76 dE between the undone and done fills, both for normal vision and for simulated protanopia and deuteranopia (Machado 2009). I also checked kidCardHTML and the kpray handler in the code.
s1.observed: Every button reads 'Prayed' with the same check icon in both states (apps/prayer.html:1587-1588). Only the fill changes (--accent-deep to --olive, :427) and the title turns muted (:407). My luminance ratios between the fills match the report exactly: Ezra 1.75 light and 1.16 dark, Kiara 1.28 light and 1.06 dark. But the hues differ strongly: normal-vision dE is 35.8 (Ezra light), 31.8 (Ezra dark), 35.8 (Kiara light) and 25.6 (Kiara dark), so a colour-typical child sees teal or ochre against green. Under colour-vision deficiency, Kiara's fills nearly merge: dark dE is 4.2 for protanopia and 10.2 for deuteranopia, light is 16.9 and 17.9. Ezra's stay distinct (dE about 32-36). The first tap marked the card; the second tap left it marked (aria-pressed true), so there is no undo. The kid's face appears under 'prayed today', but cards other people prayed also show faces, so faces do not tell 'I did it' from 'someone did'. There is no speechSynthesis in prayer.html. The header plan name depends on the plan: 'Around the table' in the light capture, 'Everything' in dark.
s1.rationale: The constitution requires kid flows to work without reading (HUB-AUDIT-PROMPT.md:118-119). Here a check-marked 'Prayed' button is shown before the child has prayed, so the icon cue says the opposite of the state, and a colour meaning has to be learned. Praying on the family list is the kids' daily Prayer flow and earns a daily star. The flow still works (tapping is harmless and idempotent, and a parent can help), so it is 'a core daily flow noticeably hampered though a workaround exists', which is medium. It is not high: nothing is wrong or unsafe.
s1.correction: 'A 4-5-year-old or a colour-blind viewer cannot tell done from not done' is overstated. For colour-typical vision the two fills differ clearly in hue (dE 26-36); only the luminance ratio is low (1.06-1.75). The near-invisible case is simulated protanopia on Kiara's dark palette (dE 4.2). The real defect is that the untapped button already shows '✓ Prayed', and no non-colour cue marks the state. The header text quoted ('· Everything') is one plan's name and is not fixed.

s2.method: Read apps/prayer.html:420-430, 1577-1591 and 1270. Recomputed the WCAG luminance ratios and CIE76 colour differences (normal vision, plus Machado deutan/protan simulation) from the fill colours. Ran my own script as Ezra and Kiara on iPad portrait in light and dark: tap one card, read its state, tap it again, screenshot.
s2.observed: The label is 'Prayed' with the same check icon before and after the tap; only aria-label changes ('I prayed for…' becomes 'Prayed for…'). The fill goes from the profile colour to olive, the title dims (46,37,29 to 117,103,91 in light, a 2.75:1 change), and the kid's own face appears under 'prayed today'. A second tap leaves done=true (setPrayed(p, true) at :1270), so a kid cannot undo. I reproduced the luminance ratios between the two fills exactly: Ezra 1.75 light / 1.16 dark, Kiara 1.28 / 1.06. The hue difference, however, is large: ΔE 35.8 / 31.8 (Ezra) and 35.8 / 25.6 (Kiara) for normal vision. Under deutan/protan simulation Ezra stays at ΔE about 32-36, while Kiara drops to 17-18 in light and 4-10 in dark. In my Kiara dark screenshot, sage-green done buttons sit clearly apart from gold not-done ones. Titles are text only: no picture and no read-aloud.
s2.rationale: The constitution requires kid flows to be completable by icon, colour and position alone (HUB-AUDIT-PROMPT.md:118-119). Here the request is text only, the button says 'Prayed' before it is tapped, colour is the only state cue on the button and nothing explains it, and a mis-tap cannot be undone (it credits the family list and the star flow). This is the kids' daily flow, and it is noticeably hampered even though tapping still works. That fits 'medium: a core daily flow is noticeably hampered though a workaround exists'. It is not high, because the flow completes and the header changes to 'You prayed for everyone today!'.
s2.correction: 'A 4-5-year-old or a colour-blind viewer cannot tell done from not done' overstates the problem. The 1.06-1.75 figures are luminance ratios, but the fills differ strongly in hue (ΔE 26-36 for normal vision; Ezra's stays at about 32 even under colour-blindness simulation), and the title also dims. Only Kiara's pair under simulated colour-blindness (ΔE 4-10 in dark) comes close to indistinguishable. The load-bearing defects are the identical label and icon, the text-only request and the lack of undo.

s1.method: I ran s1-kitchen-type.mjs on iPad landscape as Eli. It measures font size and canvas cap height for Today and Kitchen view, then converts cap height to reading distance at 0.192 mm per CSS px, using the report's comfortable rule (cap >= d/200) and a 10-arcmin minimum (cap >= d/344). I read the Kitchen CSS, which uses fixed px with no iPad media query, and checked the glanceability rule in the audit constitution.
s1.observed: Kitchen items are 24 px (cap 18), the heading 36 px (cap 26), category labels 13.5 px and the 'for' text 16.5 px. Today: h1 31 px, titles 17.5 px, meta 13.5 px, nav 12 px. Comfortable distances match the report: h1 0.88 m, title 0.50 m, meta 0.38 m, nav 0.35 m, Kitchen item 0.69 m, heading 1.0 m. At the minimum threshold, Kitchen items reach 1.19 m and the heading 1.72 m. For 2-3 m the report's own rule needs about 69-104 px font (40-61 px at the minimum), not 90-130 px. The menu label reads 'Kitchen view / Big type for the counter', and the view listed 14 items. The constitution's 2-3 m rule names key information on the always-open iPad (today's reading, running timers, leftovers expiring; HUB-AUDIT-PROMPT.md:116-117). Prayer is an app a person opens, and the resting iPad shows Home.
s1.rationale: The measurements hold, but reading an opened app at arm's length is normal, and the 2-3 m requirement targets Home's key information, not in-app Prayer screens. Kitchen view promises type 'for the counter', and it is legible at the counter (0.7-1.2 m). Its only weakness is a mild mismatch with 'big type' if it is left open as an ambient screen. That is a minor inconvenience with no information hidden or misleading, so low under the rule ('medium needs a real effect on use').
s1.correction: The '2-3 m needs roughly 90-130 px type' figure is wrong under the report's own heuristic: about 69-104 px (comfortable) or 40-61 px (minimum). 'Nothing in Prayer is legible from across the room' is true, but it is judged against a 2-3 m requirement the constitution applies to Home's key information, not to Prayer. Kitchen view is explicitly for 'the counter', where 24 px type does read.

s2.method: Read the Kitchen view CSS (apps/prayer.html:353-364) and the 'Big type for the counter' label (:1730). Measured cap heights myself by reading pixels from the 1x capture kitchen-typical-ipad-landscape-light.png, then recomputed the distances with the investigator's rule (cap height × 200, 0.192 mm per CSS px) and with a 20/20 acuity threshold (5 arcmin). That gives 0.65-0.69 m and 1.0 m under the 1:200 rule, matching layout.json (kitchenItem 0.69, kitchenH1 1.0). At 2.5 m an 18 px cap subtends about 4.75 arcmin, which is the 20/20 recognition limit. Not medium: nothing is hidden or misleading on a primary flow.

The Kitchen view promises counter distance and roughly meets it. s1.method: Read apps/prayer.html (Settings markup 503-532, load/save 630-695, L()/PL() 707-708, renderPlans 1171-1227) and the cited screenshot. Then ran my own harness script: Eli on the iPhone PWA viewed Family on Today, closed, reopened Prayer in a fresh session, went straight to Settings, recorded all visible headings and labels, changed the rotation size, and read the family-scope rows back from the Worker. s1.method: Recomputed every cited pair from the design.css token values with my own WCAG script. Answered and anniversary dates (gold on bg) 2.96, 3.24, 3.47. The 'shared' pill (teal on teal-soft) 3.98, 4.29, 3.99, with p10 down to 3.61 rendered. 'not prayed in N days' 4.05 Hearth, 4.06 Parchment, 4.33 Frost. Unpressed Mine/Family 4.45 Hearth, 4.37 Parchment, 4.55 Frost; Frost passes and was not listed. The nav label 'Record' measures 5.72 in Midnight and 5.46 in Forest, the same as List, Add and More, and token math on glass-strong gives 5.68 and 5.51. s1.rationale: The rule's medium example applies: 'text below WCAG AA' that measurably hampers reading on a primary device. In Hearth, the default palette, the Today screen that is used every day shows 13 px and 12.5 px gold labels at 2.78-2.96:1, well under 4.5. The 11 px 'shared' pill and the terra 'not prayed' line are also under AA. These are secondary labels, not the request titles, so it is not high. Removing the dark failures leaves a light-palette-only problem, which is still medium.
s1.correction: The Midnight/Forest/System-dark failures are wrong. Done row titles measure about 6.0-6.2:1, not 3.24-3.27, and the 'Record' nav label measures about 5.5-5.7:1, not 3.40-3.56. Here the 'Answered recently' label and the answered dates on Record are 2.78-3.47 in the three light palettes, including the default Hearth, on the Kitchen iPad and the phones, in a daily adult app. The shared pill (11 px) and terra 'not prayed in N days' are also under 4.5. These are secondary labels, and the main content (titles and notes) passes, so it does not rise to high. The dark-theme parts are sampling artifacts and do not add to the rating.

The done row titles in Midnight, Forest and System-dark render at about 6.1-6.2, not 3.24-3.27: the p10 came from a line box overlapping the top edge of the fixed nav. The nav 'Record' 3.40-3.56 is content showing through the unblurred nav at one scroll position, and the nav background measures 5.6 in the shell captures. s1.method: Read apps/tally.html in full and the report section, viewed the kid iPad and iPhone captures, then ran my own script (s1-reset.mjs, typical seed, WebKit) as Ezra on ipad-portrait and iphone-pwa. It measured + against Reset, tapped + five times, then tapped Reset once, and recorded the server row, dialogs, toasts and any undo control.
s1.observed: Reset's handler is `set(0)` with no guard (apps/tally.html:155). On the iPad the count went 17 to 0 on screen and on the server (12 seeded + 5). On the iPhone it went 5 to 0. Both runs showed no dialog, no toast in the frame or the shell, and no undo control. The only row left is `count`, so no history is kept. Kid geometry was the same on both devices: + is 168x168 and Reset is 162x64, with 24 px between the bottom of + and the top of Reset and 97 px of horizontal overlap, so Reset sits directly under the + a kid keeps tapping. Reset has no icon, and its fill, glass-strong background and ink are computed identical to + (rgba(255,252,248,0.84), rgb(46,37,29)). The minus button is not the same material: it uses the lighter --glass and looks visibly darker in kid-typical-ipad-portrait-light.png. Reset also differs in shape, a pill rather than a disc.
s1.rationale: Counting is Tally's primary job, and kids use it (no visibleTo). One mis-tap 24 px below the hammered + erases the count with no way to get it back. A pre-reader cannot read the only thing that marks the button as destructive. That fits medium under audits/02-shell.md:25-37: a flow noticeably hampered or broken in a way that misleads the user. It is not high, because the value is a throwaway counter in the tapper's own person scope and no household or shared data is lost.
s1.correction: Minor: "three identical-material buttons" is not exact. Only + and Reset share the glass-strong fill. The minus button uses the lighter --glass and reads darker, and Reset is a pill, not a disc. The substance still holds: nothing about Reset (no icon, no colour) signals that it destroys the count.

s2.method: Read apps/tally.html in full and the report section, then ran my own script (audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/UX-TALLY-1/s2-reset.mjs, typical seed, WebKit) as Ezra and Kiara on the iPad in portrait and as Eli on the iPhone. It measured the + and Reset geometry and computed styles, hit-tested the band below +, tapped Reset, and recorded dialogs, toasts, undo controls, and every local and server copy of the count.
