The only local copy, hub.cache.tally.person.ezra, holds v:0, so the old value is gone everywhere. Eli: 37 -> 0, the same result. Kid geometry, identical for Ezra and Kiara: + is 168x168 at y 654-822, Reset is 162x64 at y 846-910, so the gap is exactly 24 px and the two overlap horizontally by 97 px. elementFromPoint returns nothing from 0 to 20 px below + and hits Reset from 24 px down. Adult iPhone: + is 140x140, Reset is 145x44, the gap is again 24 px. + and Reset have the same computed fill: background-color rgba(255,252,248,0.84), the same spec gradient, radius 999px and ink rgb(46,37,29). Reset has no aria-label and no icon. Kiara (the other pre-reader) opens Tally too, because apps.json has no visibleTo.
s2.rationale: Medium under audits/02-shell.md:25-37. For the pre-readers (ages 4-5, audits/HUB-AUDIT-PROMPT.md:118), the destructive control is a word-only pill in the same glass as +, only 24 px below it. That makes a secondary flow (start over) misleading, and one tap loses data irreversibly with no confirm and no undo. It is not high: the value is a single throwaway counter in the tapper's own person scope. No household data, core daily job, privacy or safety is involved. It is not low: the loss is permanent, and both kids see the control on the Kitchen iPad every time they open the app.
s2.correction: One small nuance, not an error: the three buttons share the same material, but Reset is a pill with text while +/− are circles with glyphs, so they are not identical in shape. s1.method: Read apps/tally.html and hub.ready (apps/hub.js:324-368). Then ran s1-loading.mjs (typical seed, WebKit, iphone-pwa as Eli) in three cases: (A) first open on a new device with no throttling, (B) first open with the tally GET held 9 s and three taps at about 1.5-2.8 s, and (C) a reopen on the same device (cache present) with the GET still held 9 s.
s1.observed: B reproduces the report's numbers. At 1.5 s the count showed 0, the pill was empty and #plus had no handler. Three taps by 2.79 s left 0 with an empty queue. Handlers were wired at 6.17 s, when hub.ready's 6000 ms race fired (hub.js:337), with the count still 0, and it read 37 at 10.5 s. There was no aria-busy, no disabled state and no skeleton. The exposure, however, is much narrower than the headline suggests. In A, with no throttling, the buttons were wired 199 ms after navigation (11 ms after the frame loaded) and already showed 37. In C, even with the GET held 9 s, the buttons were wired at 130 ms and showed the cached 37, because hub.ready only waits when no channel has `since > 0` (hub.js:336-337). The dead-tap window therefore needs both a first-ever Tally open for that person on that device (or a cleared cache) and a slow first pull, and it lasts at most 6 s. The lost taps are also not silent: the dial visibly stays at 0.
s1.rationale: This is an edge case with a small, one-off harm: a few visibly ineffective taps, lasting at most 6 s, once per device and person, and only on a slow network. That is low under audits/02-shell.md:25-37 ("an edge case, or a minor inconvenience"). The damaging part, a live tap overwriting the real count between 6.1 s and the pull landing, is filed and counted separately as P3-TALLY-02/P3-TALLY-07, so it cannot raise this item.
s1.correction: "Taps first do nothing" holds only on the first open of Tally on a device (no tally cache) with a slow first pull. On a normal network the dead window is about 0.2 s, and on any later open it is about 0.1 s even with a 9 s held pull. The taps are also not lost "without a sign": the count visibly does not change, though there is no busy indicator. The medium rating is inflated: it should be low.

s2.method: Read apps/tally.html and hub.ready (apps/hub.js:324-369). ready() waits up to 6 s for the first pull only when the device has no cached scope (`seen` false, line 334-337). My script (audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/UX-TALLY-2/s2-loading.mjs) polled every 100 ms in three cases: (A) first open on a fresh device with the tally GET held 9 s, (B) first open on a fresh device with no hold, (C) a second open on the same device with a cache, still held.
s2.observed: A: #plus had no handler until 6.33 s, and the pill stayed empty until then. Three taps at 1.59, 2.16 and 3.04 s left the count at 0 with an empty queue; the server kept 37. The count read 0 with the buttons live from 6.33 s until the pull landed at 9.26 s, when it read 37. At no point was there aria-busy, a skeleton, a spinner or a disabled/aria-disabled state. The shell's sync state read 'synced' from 0.42 s while the tally GET was still held, so there is no sign anywhere. B, a normal link: the buttons were live and 37 was shown by 0.23 s. C, cached: 37 and live buttons at the first sample (0.11 s), even with the GET held. The investigator's numbers (dead through 2.8 s, live at 6.1 s, 37 by the 10.5 s sample) match mine within sampling.
s2.rationale: Low under audits/02-shell.md:25-37, lower than the investigator's medium: this is an edge case. The dead-tap window only exists the first time a profile opens Tally on a device and only while that first pull is slow. Every later open resolves from cache in about 0.1 s (C), and on a normal link the window is about 0.2 s (B). The taps that go dead are also the harmless part, because a dead tap cannot overwrite the count. The damaging part, live taps writing over the real count from 6 s on and the fake 0, is already filed as P3-TALLY-02 (critical) and P3-TALLY-07. What is left for this ID, no busy state and a few lost taps on a first slow load, is a minor inconvenience with narrow exposure: a new device, a new guest, or a cleared cache on a slow link.
s2.correction: No factual error. The item omits the key exposure detail: the dead window happens only on the first open per device and profile (no cached tally scope, apps/hub.js:334-337). Cached opens are live at about 0.1 s even with a slow network. The item's 10.5 s figure is a sample time; the pull actually landed at about 9.2 s, which matches the correction that the 0 lasts until the pull lands.

s1.method: Read apps.json:7, index.html widgetHtml (685-692) and enterShell (620-628), and the Tally report's own jobs table. Ran my own script against the local rig (WebKit, typical seed) as Eli on iPhone PWA and Ezra on iPad portrait. For each I checked Home for any Tally content, then tapped Apps, the Tally tile and +, and reloaded with the hash the shell left behind.
s1.observed: For both people it took 3 taps (Apps tab, Tally tile, +): Eli went 37 to 38 and Ezra 12 to 13. Home had no Tally text or button. Its [data-open] targets were f260, leftovers and prayer for Eli and only kidverse for Ezra. The kid Home's 'Let's play — open your apps' card is just another way into Apps. widgetHtml has a branch only for f260, and Tally is tile 'small', so no count appears anywhere outside the app. After opening Tally the shell's hash is #tally, and a reload with that hash reopens Tally directly (enterShell index.html:627). So a PWA resumed or relaunched with the hash needs 1 tap, not 3. Each extra count in a burst is 1 tap.
s1.rationale: The facts hold (3 taps, no Home card or widget), but the rating is inflated. The report's own jobs table (tally.md, section 1) rates counting 'Occasionally, in bursts', so it is not a core daily flow. It is not broken either: opening takes 2 taps, like every non-card app (02-shell.md:605), and then one tap per count. The Phase 4 rubric penalises only 4 or more taps (EOU-5). 3 taps only misses a +1 bonus (EOU-1). That is a minor inconvenience on an occasional tool, so it is low under the rule, not the medium that needs a core daily flow noticeably hampered or a secondary flow broken.
s1.correction: The item says counting 'misses the brief's target' as if this were a defect. EOU-1 (04-design-system.md:193) is a +1 bonus criterion, and the penalty rule EOU-5 only fires at 4 or more taps, so 3 taps is neutral under the house rubric. Calling '+' the household's most frequent job overstates it: the report's own jobs table says counting is occasional. The item also leaves out that the shell reopens straight into Tally when the #tally hash survives (index.html:625-627), which cuts repeat use to 1 tap.
citations: audits/03-apps/tally.md (section 1, jobs table: 'Occasionally, in bursts of many taps')

s1.method: Recomputed the WCAG ratios from the RGB samples in themes.json by hand. Then ran my own pixel script on standalone tally.html (iPad portrait, WebKit) in Midnight, Forest and System on a dark OS, for Eli, Dad, Kiara and Ezra. It measured each disc's fill against the wash, the strongest rim, ring or shadow pixel against the wash (16 radii, from 6 px inside to 10 px outside the edge), the glyph against the disc, and the dial against the wash. This WebKit paints no backdrop-filter blur; the wash behind is a smooth gradient, so blur should change the fill little, but real iOS glass was not seen.
s1.observed: My recomputed figures match the investigator's, for example Eli Midnight − 1.20 and + 1.26, Kiara + 1.62, Dad − 1.18. In my own run the − fill against the wash matched themes.json exactly: 1.13 (Dad) to 1.45 (Kiara), in all three dark cases. For +, my wash sample fell in the gap between the buttons and gave 1.03-1.10, so I rely on the investigator's 1.17-1.62, sampled left of −. No edge pixel reaches 3:1 either: the rim and ring peak at 1.62-1.97 against the wash. The dial is 1.23-1.81 against the wash. The glyphs that identify the buttons are 11.2-13.8:1 against their disc. In the screenshots (Midnight and Ezra's teal, Forest and Eli's navy) the discs read clearly as three dark circles with bright + and − glyphs. Eli's navy is the subtlest. The look is a dark-on-dark brown or navy scheme, not a glowing pastel.
s1.rationale: Under the rule, a visual item is medium only if it misleads, hides information, or measurably hampers reading or tapping on a primary device. None of that happens here. The controls are 96-168 px, their glyphs are about 12:1, and every text passes AA. WCAG 1.4.11 requires 3:1 only for the visual information needed to identify a component. Here the + and − glyphs do that, so a low fill-to-page ratio is not a 1.4.11 failure. What remains is an aesthetic weakness (muddy, low-luminance discs that do not show the person's colour), which is low. Exposure: anyone using Midnight, Forest, or System at night, on every device.
s1.correction: The item presents 3:1 as the target the disc fill fails. But the + and − glyphs identify the buttons at 11-14:1, so the fill-to-wash ratio is not the WCAG 1.4.11 measure, and the buttons do not 'barely stand out' in practice. They are plainly visible as discs, only low in luminance contrast. The item's own claim that they are 'told apart only by their ring and shadow' is also inexact: the ring and shadow peak at under 2:1, and it is the bright glyph plus the hue and chroma difference from the coloured wash that carry them. The fill figures themselves are correct.

s2.method: Recomputed two fill ratios from the RGB values in themes.json myself. Ran my own WebKit script (audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/VIS-TALLY-1/s2-edge.mjs) on the local rig to sample the fill, the left edge (±6 px) and the top edge of −, + and the dial against the wash, in Midnight, Forest, System-dark and System-light. Viewed the full-size dark iPad screenshots.
s2.observed: Recomputed from the themes.json RGB values: Dad/Midnight − fill against the wash is 1.13:1 and Kiara + is 1.62:1. That matches the report's 1.13-1.45 (−) and 1.17-1.62 (+). My run gives dark-palette fill against wash of 1.13-1.43 (−), 1.00-1.08 (+, sampled at mid-height) and 1.22-1.85 (dial). The best edge pixel reaches only 1.20-2.23:1, and the top sheen edge 1.55-2.44:1, so no boundary reaches 3:1. In System-light the same edges reach 3.2-5.3:1. But the glyphs that identify the controls are high contrast: + is 11.79-13.3:1 and − is 10.43-12.44:1, and the count is 10.98-12.26:1 in every dark row of themes.json. All targets are 96, 140 or 168 px. In main- and kid-typical-ipad-portrait-dark.png the three discs read clearly as distinct round shapes, with a hue difference (brown-black on navy or teal) and a drop shadow. WebKit paints no backdrop-filter blur; the wash is a smooth gradient, so a real blur would change the fill little.
s2.rationale: The measured luminance contrast is real and reproducible. But WCAG 1.4.11 does not require a button's fill or boundary to reach 3:1 when its label identifies the control, and here the + and − glyphs and the count are over 10:1. The discs are also plainly visible in the screenshots. Nothing is hidden or misleading, reading is not hampered, and targets are far above 44 px. The rule's bar for a medium visual item ('misleads, hides information, or measurably hampers reading or tapping') is not met. This is an aesthetic weakness (muddy, low-glow dark look), so low.
s2.correction: The ratios are right, but 'the non-text target is 3:1' misapplies WCAG 1.4.11: the high-contrast +/− glyphs (10.4-13.3:1) identify the controls, so the fill does not need 3:1. 'Barely stand out' overstates it; the discs are clearly visible shapes. The item says the dial too, but only the buttons were measured (the dial measures 1.22-1.85:1). Severity should be low, not medium.

s1.method: I read apps/timer.html in full and wrote s1-preset-cancels.mjs (WebKit, real clock, typical seed). In it, Eli's iPhone PWA runs the Timer and Eli's iPad sits on Home showing the pill. The script taps a preset chip, then Reset, while a timer runs, and does the same for Ezra on an iPhone. It counts window.confirm calls and reads the server row, the shell toast and the iPad pill after an explicit hub.pull().
s1.observed: Running at 9:55 with Pause, server timer.active={endAt,total:600,...}, iPad pill 9:55. One tap on '3 min' gave 3:00 / Start (primary) at once. The server row became timer.active:null and lastPreset:180, the iPad pill went null after its pull, the shell showed no toast, there was no undo and confirm was called 0 times. Reset while running (2:58) gave the same result: 3:00 Start and a null row. For Ezra (data-kind=kid) the chips stay enabled while running (0 disabled). The 30 min chip ends at y=678 and Pause starts at y=694, a 16 px gap (chips 64 px tall, Pause 84 px). One chip tap cancelled his 4:59 timer too (row null). The adult B_measure gap also recomputes to 686-(626+44)=16 px.
s1.rationale: Medium: a secondary flow is misleading and the running countdown is lost for good. There is only one timer, so the natural kitchen move of tapping '3 min' for eggs while a 10 min timer runs silently kills the first timer on every device of that person. Nothing warns, and the remaining time cannot be recovered. It is not high because the tapper sees the change at once, the targets meet 44 px with a 16 px gap (accidental taps are not especially likely), and restarting is a workaround.

s2.method: I read apps/timer.html and the shell timer code in index.html (lines 773-828). I then ran my own WebKit rig script with Eli on an iPhone PWA and Eli on an iPad: I started a 10 min timer on the phone, confirmed the iPad pill, tapped the "3 min" chip once, and read the phone app, the server row and the iPad pill after a pull. I also started a timer as the kid Ezra, measured the chips and tapped one while it ran.
s2.observed: Before the tap the phone read 9:56 with Pause, the server held timer.active {endAt, total:600}, and the iPad pill read 9:56. One tap on "3 min" gave 3:00 with Start (primary) and ring --p 1.0000. The server row became timer.active: null (lastPreset 180), and after a pull the iPad pill was gone (null). No dialog fired, nothing offered an undo, and 0 chips were disabled while the timer ran. On the iPhone (430x884) the second chip row sits at y 626 with height 44, so it ends at y 670, and Pause starts at y 686: a 16 px gap, matching basics.json B_measure. In kid mode the chips are 64 px tall, the last row ends at y 678 and Pause starts at y 694 (again 16 px). One chip tap as Ezra while 4:59 was running gave 1:00 Start. The code matches: the preset handler calls stop(); write(null) (apps/timer.html:121-125), and Reset does the same (apps/timer.html:120).
s2.rationale: The kitchen timer is a daily flow. A single tap on a 44 px chip 16 px above Pause cancels it on every device of that person, and the remaining time cannot be recovered. On the shared Kitchen iPad a stray or child's tap during cooking loses the timer, so the alarm never fires. A workaround exists (notice it, restart it, re-estimate the time), so this is 'a core daily flow noticeably hampered though a workaround exists', which is medium. It is not high: the change is visible at once to whoever tapped, and the chips are a reasonable size and distance apart.
s2.correction: No factual error. One framing note: Reset clearing the timer without a confirm is expected, because Reset is an explicit cancel control. The real problem is only the preset chips.

s1.method: I wrote s1-pause.mjs (WebKit, real clock). Eli has the Timer open on both an iPhone PWA and the iPad. The phone starts 10 min, both show it running, then the phone pauses. The script compares the computed styles of the paused dial with the idle 10:00 dial, pulls on the iPad, then goes to Home and reopens the Timer on the phone.
s1.observed: Paused at 9:50: the button is 'Start' with class btn-primary, the body class is 'ds' and the dial class 'dial glass', the same as idle. Time colour, opacity (1), animation (none), ring stroke and ring opacity (1) are all identical to the idle 10:00 state, and the page text has no 'Paused' anywhere. The only difference is the ring's --p=0.9833 (a small gap at 12 o'clock), which is the same progress cue a running timer shows. Server after the pause: timer.active:null. The iPad after its pull showed 10:00 / Start with --p=1, reset to the full preset. On the phone the Home pill and chip were null while paused, and reopening the Timer showed 10:00 Start: the 9:50 is lost.
s1.rationale: Medium: a secondary flow (pause) is broken and misleading. The pause survives only while that one page stays open. Other devices reset to the full preset and the Home pill vanishes, so a paused timer looks like no timer at all, and the paused dial carries no paused cue. It is not high: a workaround exists (remember the time and restart), and the core start-to-alarm flow works.
s1.correction: 'Styled exactly like an idle timer of that length' is slightly overstated. The paused ring keeps its partial progress (--p = left/total, 0.9833 at 9:50 of 10:00), while an idle dial's ring is always full. That partial ring is the same thing a running timer shows, so it is not a pause cue, but the paused dial is not pixel-identical to an idle one. Everything else holds: no 'Paused' label, no dimming or blink, a primary 'Start', and state lost on other devices and on reopen.

s2.method: I used the same WebKit rig run as for UX-TIMER-1 (the script is in the UX-TIMER-1 folder and writes its P2 output to UX-TIMER-2/s2). The phone (Eli) ran a 10 min timer with Eli's iPad Timer app open. I paused the phone, then read the phone app, the server row and the iPad app after a pull. Next I left the phone app for Home, checked the pill, and reopened the Timer. I compared the paused styling with the code and with audits/screens/timer/paused-typical-ipad-portrait-light.png.
s2.observed: Before the pause the iPad Timer showed 9:56 / Pause. The phone paused at 9:50 with button text 'Start', btn-primary set, no 'Paused' or 'Resume' text anywhere, and ring --p 0.9833. The server row became timer.active: null. About 4 s later, after a pull, the iPad showed 10:00 / Start with --p 1.0000, meaning it had reset (apps/timer.html:134-135). The phone's Home pill was null. Reopening the Timer on the phone showed 10:00 / Start, so the 9:50 was lost. This matches basics.json D_* (2:55 paused, reopened at 3:00) and sync2.json S2 (9:28, then the iPad at 10:00 24 s later). The paused and idle states are not identical, though: the ring keeps the remaining fraction. The audit screen of 6:20 paused on a 15 min timer shows an arc of about 42% under a highlighted '15 min' chip, whereas an idle timer always shows a full ring whose time matches the highlighted chip.
s2.rationale: Pause is a secondary flow. It works only while that one iframe stays open. Leaving the app, or pausing on another device, silently throws away the remaining time, and other devices show a reset timer. This is 'a secondary flow broken or misleading', which is medium. It is not high: pausing is not the core countdown, and the person can restart with a guessed time.
s2.correction: 'Styled exactly like an idle timer' overstates it. A paused timer keeps a partial ring (--p = left/total, for example about 42% for 6:20 of 15:00), and its digits differ from the highlighted preset chip. An idle timer always shows a full ring. What is missing is any explicit cue: no 'Paused' label, no dimming, and the button reads 'Start' rather than 'Resume'. A pause early in a timer (0.98 ring at 9:50 of 10:00) does look almost identical to idle. The 24 s iPad delay in sync2 is simply pull timing: here the iPad reset about 4 s after pausing, on its next pull.

s1.method: I wrote s1-missed-end.mjs (WebKit iPhone PWA, Eli, installClock, probes for beeps and notifications). It models suspension differently from the investigator: document.hidden is forced true, then clock.setSystemTime jumps the wall clock without firing any due timer (closer to how iOS suspends a page), then the page is made visible again. It ran four cases: Timer closed and back 2 min after 0; back 30 s after 0, then a simulated notification tap (location.hash='#timer', which is what the SW 'open' message does); Timer open and back 2 min after 0; whole page closed and reopened on #timer 2 min after 0.
s1.observed: Back 2 min after 0 with the Timer closed: no pill, no toast, 0 oscillators, 0 notifications, and the server row cleared. Opening the Timer then showed '1:00 Start', not done. Back 30 s after 0: beep (3 oscillators), toast 'Timer done — 1:00 is up.' and notification 'Timer done / 1:00 is up.'. After the simulated notification tap the Timer showed the idle '1:00 Start', not the done state, because the shell had already removed the record. Timer open and back 2 min after 0: the app shows the blinking done state 0:00 and plays its three-note beep late (3 oscillators), while the shell shows no toast or notification. Page closed and reopened 2 min after 0: '1:00 Start', no pill or toast, row null.
s1.rationale: Medium: a secondary flow (missed-alarm recovery) is misleading. After more than 60 s nothing says the timer ran out or when, and even the one alert that does fire opens the Timer on an idle preset. Exposure is the common phone case: a timer started and the phone locked (a suspended iOS page cannot beep, and the timer has no server push). The 24/7 Kitchen iPad, which stays awake, is mostly unaffected. It is not high: the missing alert at the moment of expiry is a platform limit, and the vanished pill lets the user infer the timer ended.

s2.method: I wrote my own Chromium rig script with installClock, the Phase 3 audio and notification probes, and hidden emulated by forcing document.hidden and then running clock.fastForward. It covers four cases for a 1 min timer on Eli's iPhone PWA. R1: on Home, hidden through the end, back 30 s after 0. R2: the same, back about 2 min after 0. R3: Timer open, page closed, reopened on #timer 2 min after 0. R4: Home visible at 0, then location.hash='#timer' (what the service worker's 'open' message does) to follow the notification tap. I also read index.html:797-828, sw.js:62-68 and index.html:1573-1575, and checked verify-critic-locked-phone-no-alert-2-1.json S2_appOpen.
s2.observed: R1 (back 30 s after the end) gave 1 AudioContext with 3 oscillators, a toast 'Timer done — 1:00 is up.' and one 'Timer done' notification: the shell's 60 s grace window works (index.html:806). R2 (back about 2 min after) gave no audio (0 oscillators), no toast, no notification and no pill; the server row was null and nothing on Home mentioned the timer. R3 showed 1:00 / Start / done=false with no toast or pill, the same as B6. In R4 the shell beeped, toasted and notified at 0 and removed the record in the same call. Following the tap to #timer then showed 1:00 / Start, idle rather than the done state, which confirms by run what the report had only by code. In the Phase 3 S2_appOpen evidence the open app showed done with 3 oscillators only 'back' after the lock, and the shell sent no notification.
s2.rationale: On a phone, a timer running out while the phone is locked or the app is closed is the normal case, since iOS suspends the PWA. More than 60 s after the end, nothing tells the person it ended or how long ago, and reopening the Timer shows its preset at 'Start', which reads as though it never ran. That is 'a secondary flow misleading' and hampers the daily timer on the phone, so medium. It is not high: the missed alarm itself is a separate verified defect, the Kitchen iPad on Home stays awake and alerts normally, and inside 60 s the shell does beep, toast and notify.
s2.correction: No substantive error. A precision note: the shell does not clear every ended record silently. A record seen within 60 s of its end still gets the beep, toast and notification (index.html:806-810), so 'no trace' applies only to a return more than 60 s after the end. The notification-tap path, filed 'by code, not run', now reproduces: #timer opens on the idle '1:00 Start'.

s1.method: Read apps/timer.html in full and visual.mjs's V4 code, then ran my own WebKit rig script (Elizabeth, iPad portrait, in the hub viewer). It pushed a 6 s timer to the end, froze the blink at both phases, recorded the computed paint and screenshotted each state. I sampled pixels from the existing screenshots and computed WCAG luminance ratios myself.
s1.observed: True: at 0 the page text is exactly 'Kitchen timer 0:00 1 min 3 min 5 min 10 min 15 min 30 min Start Reset', with 0 aria-live/role=alert/status elements and no 'Time's up' word or icon (finish() at timer.html:102 only toggles classes). Not true that the cue is colour only, and V4's number measures an invisible element. At done `.dial.empty .ring .fg` has opacity 0 (timer.html:30, measured opacity '0'), so V4's 'done ring' rgb(188,90,56) is never painted. What shows is the bg track, color-mix(danger 55%) = rgb(211,153,130), drawn as a full uniform ring with no progress arc. Against the running arc rgb(138,106,75) that is 2.04:1 (V4 says 1.1), and 1.65:1 against the running track. The digits go from rgb(99,76,54) to rgb(188,90,56), a 1.78:1 luminance step. The blink is steps(2) over 1 s, measured at 1 then 0.65 opacity, not 0.3. A colour-blind or across-the-room viewer is not left with colour alone. The missing words or icon and the subtle 0.65 blink are polish. The real threat to this job is the likely-silent iOS beep, which is a separate unresolved item. The medium rule's 'core daily flow noticeably hampered' is not met by the visual state on its own.
s1.correction: 'Only by colour' is wrong: the blink (a luminance/opacity change), the full ring in place of the progress arc (a shape change), 0:00, and Start returning as the primary button are all non-colour cues. The 1.1 and 1.9 luminance ratios (V4) compare the fg stroke, which has opacity 0 in the done state. The visible done ring vs the running arc is 2.04:1 in Hearth for Elizabeth. The blink's dim phase is opacity 0.65, not 0.3, because steps(2) never reaches the 0.3 keyframe.

s1.method: Ran my own WebKit rig script as Elizabeth in the hub viewer on the rig iPad in portrait and landscape. It measured the rendered digits' ink height with canvas measureText on the computed font, the dial box, and the uncapped min(82vw, 52vh) value. I converted to mm at 132 CSS px per inch (264 ppi at 2x) and computed reading distances under several legibility rules.
s1.observed: Font 87.84 px (24cqw of a 400 px dial less padding), weight 300. Ink height is 64 px for '0' and 63 px for the '5:47' string, which is 12.3 mm, matching the report. Portrait: the frame is 820x1132 and the uncapped dial would be 589 px, so the 400 px cap binds (266 px free below the buttons, 250 px above). Landscape: the frame is 1180x772, so 52vh = 401 px and the dial is 400x400. There the height limit, not the 400 px cap, sets the size, and removing the cap would gain 1 px. Distance for 12.3 mm: 2.46 m by d/200, 1.48 m by d/120, 4.93 m by d/400, and 8.47 m at the 5-arcmin 20/20 threshold. The rig's font is a Windows fallback for ui-rounded; SF Pro Rounded on a real iPad has a similar numeral height (about 0.7 em), which I did not measure on a device.
s1.rationale: The low rule applies: this is a minor inconvenience. 12 mm numerals are about microwave-display size. A normal-sighted adult can read them at 3 m (threshold about 8.5 m); d/200 is a comfort guideline, not a limit. Glancing from across the kitchen is somewhat hampered by the thin weight-300 strokes, but it is not 'noticeably hampered' in the sense the medium rule needs. The exposure is the Kitchen iPad Timer screen only; the fix gain exists only in portrait.
s1.correction: 'Both iPad orientations get a 400 px dial because of the cap' is wrong for landscape: 52vh of the 772 px viewer frame is 401 px, so the height limits the dial there and removing the cap changes nothing. The cap binds only in portrait, where the uncapped dial would be 589 px (digits about 18 mm). 'Reads only to about 2.5 m' presents the d/200 comfort rule as a hard limit; by acuity the digits are legible well beyond 3 m.

s1.method: I read apps/timer.html:93-102 and index.html:773-828, then wrote and ran my own probe (Chromium, typical seed, real server clock, controllable browser clock, iPad portrait, Eli). It wraps AudioContext to record every oscillator's scheduled start and stop, in two cases: the Timer app open at 0 (A), and the app closed with Home showing at 0 (B). I sampled state at the end, and again +1.5 s, +3.5 s, +4.5 s and +3 min later.
s1.observed: Both the app and the shell play exactly 3 oscillators at 880 Hz, scheduled 0-0.25 s, 0.3-0.55 s and 0.6-0.85 s, so the sound lasts 0.85 s. 3 minutes later there is still 1 context and 3 oscillators in either case, so the sound never repeats. In A the done state stays: body.done, the 'blink' animation on the digits and a red wash, until Reset, Start or a preset is tapped. In B the toast 'Timer done — 1:00 is up.' is gone by +3.5 to +4.5 s (the code sets 4000 ms at index.html:810). 3 minutes later Home shows no trace of the finished timer: no pill, no card (screenshot B-home-3min-after-end-ipad.png). There is no Stop or +1 min control anywhere. Side note: in 2 of my 3 case-A runs the running timer went back to 1:00 / Start before 0 with no beep. The third run finished normally. This looks like an artifact of the accelerated browser clock running against the real server clock, and I did not attribute it to the app.
s1.rationale: This is job 3 ('notice that time is up'), a core flow used several times a day around meals. A single 0.85 s pip is easy to miss in a noisy kitchen or from another room. If the app is not in front, nothing lasts beyond a 4 s toast. That makes the flow noticeably hampered. A partial workaround exists: when the app is open, the red blinking screen stays until tapped. That matches medium under the rule's 'a core daily flow is noticeably hampered though a workaround exists'. It is not high, because the alert does fire and the in-app visual state persists. The possible iOS silence is a separate, unresolved item, and it does not raise this one.
s1.correction: Small caveat: 'needs no acknowledgement' holds for the sound only. The in-app done state (red wash, blinking digits) does wait for a tap. Also, if notification permission was granted through the Me push switch, the shell's 'Timer done' system notification (index.html:797-802) can stay in Notification Center after the toast. So 'only the blinking digits remain' is slightly overstated for that case.

s2.method: I read apps/timer.html (beep/finish) and the shell's timer block in index.html, then ran my own local-rig probe (Chromium for a real AudioContext, Kitchen iPad landscape, Eli, controllable clock). It logged every oscillator start and sampled the toast every 500 ms, with the app open (A) and with it closed on Home (B), for 3 minutes past zero.
s2.observed: A (app open): 1 AudioContext and 3 oscillator starts, all 880 Hz, scheduled at offsets 0 / 0.3 / 0.6 s, each 250 ms (0.85 s in total). Three minutes later there were still only 3 starts and no toast. The digits showed 0:00 with body.done (blinking) until Reset. B (app closed, Home): the shell played the same 3 pips once. The toast 'Timer done — 1:00 is up.' was present in the samples from 1.0 s to 4.5 s and gone at 5.0 s, which matches toast(…, 4000) at index.html:810. The pill cleared at 0. Three minutes later Home showed no trace of the timer (screenshot). Nothing has to be acknowledged and nothing repeats. This matches B3/B4 in background.json. Separately, the P3 evidence (verify-beep-silent-on-ios-3.json) found this WebKit build has no AudioContext at all, so on iOS even the single beep may not sound, which makes the gap worse.
s2.rationale: This is a feature gap in a secondary but real job: a kitchen timer is meant to get your attention. A single 0.85 s chirp, or a 4 s toast when the app is closed, is easily missed on the 24/7 Kitchen iPad by anyone across the room or at a noisy hob. The only fallback is to keep watching the screen, so the job is noticeably hampered, but it is not a core daily hub flow. That fits medium in the severity rule ('a core daily flow is noticeably hampered though a workaround exists' / 'a secondary job needs a clumsy workaround'). It is not high: the timer is not one of the household's core daily flows, and there is no kid-safety impact.
s2.correction: 'Only the blinking digits remain, and only in the app' is slightly incomplete. When the app is closed and notification permission has already been granted through the Me push switch, the shell also shows a local 'Timer done' notification (index.html:797-803; my run B recorded it). That notification stays in the OS notification list. It still does not repeat or need acknowledgement, so the substance stands.

s1.method: I read apps/timer.html in full and checked worker/src/chat.js for any timer tool. Then I wrote and ran my own WebKit probe (typical seed, real clock, Eli on iPhone). It lists every control in the app frame, starts 10 min, taps the 3 min chip while that timer runs, and reads the server's timer scope.
s1.observed: The frame has 8 buttons: 6 preset chips (60, 180, 300, 600, 900 and 1800 s, all 44 px tall) plus Start and Reset (60 px). It has 0 inputs, selects, textareas or contenteditables, and the dial and digits are not editable or tappable. So only 1, 3, 5, 10, 15 and 30 min can be set. 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 12, 20, 25, 40, 45 and 60 min cannot. With 10 min running (9:58, server timer.active total 600), tapping '3 min' showed 3:00 / Start, and the server then held timer.active = null and lastPreset = 180. The pill and chip were hidden. So a second preset replaces the running timer instead of adding one next to it. The code uses a single key, ACTIVE = 'timer.active' (apps/timer.html:80). There is no +1 min, label, sound choice or recents list. chat.js has no timer tool, only generic set_data.
s1.rationale: Job 1 (start a cooking countdown) runs several times a day. Common cooking times such as 12, 20 or 45 min cannot be set directly, and two simultaneous dishes cannot be timed. The workarounds are clumsy: chain presets (for example 10 + 1 + 1, or 30 + 15), use a second person's profile for a second timer, or leave the hub for the device's own Clock app. That fits medium ('needs a clumsy workaround', and also 'a core daily flow noticeably hampered though a workaround exists'). It is not high, because preset timing works and a chain or a native timer covers the job.
s1.correction: One minor nuance: the app does remember one last-used preset per person (lastPreset, apps/timer.html:81,124), which is a one-item 'recent'. A second concurrent timer is possible, but only under another person's profile, because the record is per person. Neither changes the substance.

s2.method: I read all of apps/timer.html, apps.json and worker/src/chat.js, looking for any custom-time, label or multi-timer path. In the same local-rig run I listed the Timer's DOM controls on the iPad and tested whether pausing a 15-minute timer at 12:00 lets you reach 12 minutes.
s2.observed: The Timer has exactly 6 presets (60/180/300/600/900/1800 s), 0 input/select/textarea/contenteditable elements, and 8 buttons in total (the 6 chips, Start, Reset). There is one person-scope record, timer.active (line 80), so a second simultaneous timer is impossible for the same person. The code has no +1 min, no label, no sound choice and no recents list. The only memory is lastPreset (lines 81 and 124), which remembers the last chip used. chat.js has no timer tool; generic set_data could write timer.active in theory, but nothing prompts the model to. Workaround: starting 15 min and pausing at 12:00, then pressing Start, resumed from 12:00 (observed 12:00, then 11:59). So a single 12-minute timer is reachable, but clumsily (wait 3 minutes and pause at the right second). Anything over 30 minutes needs a finished timer to be restarted.
s2.rationale: This is a feature gap in a secondary job (kitchen timing). Arbitrary durations need a clumsy workaround (pause trick, or chaining presets for anything over 30 min). A second concurrent timer (pizza plus oven) cannot be done at all for the signed-in person. That meets the rule's medium line: 'a secondary job cannot be done, or needs a clumsy workaround'. It is not high, because the timer is not a core daily hub flow, and everyone has the phone's own Clock app as an alternative.
s2.correction: Minor points only. 'Recents' is not wholly absent: the app remembers the last preset (lastPreset, lines 81 and 124), though that is not a list of recent durations. A lone 12-minute time can be reached with the pause trick (start 15, pause at 12:00, Start resumes), so only the pizza-plus-oven pair truly cannot be set. The report also leaves out the stronger limit that nothing above 30 minutes can be set directly.

s1.method: Read rate() and render() in apps/verses.html and hub.toast in apps/hub.js. I wrote my own script (s1-undo.mjs) that runs Eli on the iPhone PWA on the local rig. It measures the rating buttons, rates the first card Not yet as a stand-in for a mis-tap, records the recall row before and after (local and server), looks for any undo control and checks what 'Practise one anyway' offers once the queue is empty.
s1.observed: At 390 px the ratings are stacked in the order Not yet (y 293), Almost (365), Got it (437), each 364×60 with 12 px gaps (confirmed). Got it sits two buttons below Not yet, with 84 px between Not yet's bottom edge and Got it's top; the adjacent mis-tap is Almost. On the iPad the three sit in a row with Almost in the middle. Rating Not yet on 33-0 changed {box 3, due 2026-09-22, streak 2} to {s 'not', box 2, due 2026-09-24, streak 0}, and the server holds the same. The toast 'Not yet — Luke 14:26-27 again tomorrow' has 0 controls and hides after 2.2 s (hub.js:431-434). No undo, back or change control exists, and the card advanced to 36-1. The per-verse streak that gets zeroed is not shown anywhere in the UI: only the day streak from the log is shown, and scheduling uses box, not streak. F260 reads only recall.s.

A mis-tap moves one verse down one box, so it comes back for review a few days early (here due in 2 days instead of 7 in box 4). The next correct Got it moves it back up, nothing visible is lost, and the likelier adjacent slip (Almost) only holds the box. Under 'low: cosmetic, an edge case, or a minor inconvenience' (audits/02-shell.md:25-37) this is low, not medium. It does not noticeably hamper the daily review. The exposure is somewhat higher on the iPhone, where a double tap already carries over to the next card (P3-VERSES-12, low).
s1.correction: 'A thumb on Not yet instead of Got it' is not the adjacent slip: Almost sits between them on both the phone (stacked, 84 px apart) and the iPad (row). 'Zeroes its streak' is true in storage, but that per-verse streak is never displayed and does not drive scheduling, so the real cost is only an earlier review of one verse. Severity is inflated: this is low, not medium. The cited range apps/verses.html:294-304 lies inside rate(), which runs 290-306.

s2.method: Read rate() and render() in apps/verses.html and hub.toast in apps/hub.js. I wrote a pure-Node script that pulls INTERVALS out of the shipped file and recomputes every mis-tap pair from boxes 1 to 5. I checked the button gap against design.css and the rated iPhone screenshot.
s2.observed: rate() overwrites f260.recall[cur] and advances, and it keeps no previous value (verses.html:294-304). hub.toast(msg, 2200) takes no action argument (hub.js:431-434). 'undo' does not appear in verses.html. 'Practise one anyway' reopens only laterIds[0], which is not necessarily the verse you just rated. The rating buttons are separated by gap var(--sp-3) = 12px, stacked below 560 px, and each is at least 60 px tall (84 px for kids); the iPhone screenshot shows a gap of about 13 px. Recomputed costs: meaning Got it but tapping Not yet from box 5 gives box 4, due in 7 days instead of 14. From box 3 it gives box 2, due in 2 days instead of 7. The reverse slip (meaning Not yet, tapping Got it) pushes a verse you did not know out by 5 to 7 days. The glass copies are identical today, so any drift is only prospective. Weight drift is a hierarchy nuance with no measured effect on reading or tapping. Under the visual/consistency rule, medium needs a real effect on use, so this is low (info is arguable).
s1.correction: The counts hold (25 saturate copies, 16/18 breakpoints). The 'why it matters' overstates the risk. Overlays from different areas cannot collide, because apps live in separate iframe documents with their own stacking contexts. The hand-copied glass has not diverged. Medium is inflated for a no-impact token gap.

s1.method: Ran the item's grep myself across index.html, apps/*.html and apps/design.css, and searched for rem/em font sizes and any text-size setting in the shell, hub.js and design.css. Read F260's .big rule and its toggle, then recomputed the 1.15 zoom figures from remeasure-live-f260-zoom.json. Checked every viewport meta for whether pinch zoom is still allowed.
s1.observed: The -apple-system-* grep returns nothing (rc=1). No font size anywhere uses rem or em. The only relative sizes are clamp(px, vw) on display titles (index.html:97-175, kidverse:36-37, timer:31 and others). The only text-size code is design.css:293, `text-size-adjust:100%`. hub.js and index.html have no text-size preference. F260 has `.big{zoom:1.15}` (f260.html:50), toggled on body by paintSize (:2034) and stored under K.big='f260.big'. Its week label is `.tring .rn small{font-size:9.5px}` (f260.html:133). 9.5 x 1.15 = 10.925 and 28.11 x 1.15 = 32.33, matching the evidence (10.92, 32.33 x 10.92); 17 becomes 19.55 and 25 becomes 28.75. The workarounds the item does not mention: no viewport meta sets user-scalable=no, so pinch zoom works, and iOS Display Zoom, Accessibility Zoom or desktop browser zoom scale the px layout. The rig's own TV screenshot lists a 'Grandma Jo' profile, so older readers are a real audience.
s1.rationale: This is a feature gap. Larger text is a secondary need for most people but a daily one for an older reader, and today it takes a clumsy workaround: pinch-zooming every screen, or OS-wide Display Zoom. That fits 'a secondary job … needs a clumsy workaround' = medium. It is not high, because the core flows remain usable at the default sizes and workarounds exist.
s1.correction: The item says F260's page zoom is 'the only control'. Pinch zoom (no user-scalable=no in any viewport meta), iOS Display Zoom or Accessibility Zoom, and desktop browser zoom also enlarge the hub. They are clumsy, which supports medium, but they are workarounds the item should name. Minor: the zoom is on the `.big` class toggled on body; there is no `body.big` selector in the CSS.

s1.method: Wrote and ran audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/VIS-TYPE-1/s1-tv-sizes.mjs on the local harness (WebKit, device 'tv', profile tv). It records the computed font sizes and the kiosk tokens at 1920x1080 and again at 1920x1000. I also read the cited CSS and recomputed the 55-inch/65-inch iPad-equivalent arithmetic.
s1.observed: At 1920x1080 the kiosk tokens are --fs-xs 12px (not remapped), --fs-sm 18px, --fs-md 22px and --fs-lg 26px. The date #tv-date renders at 12px/700 ('Tuesday, September 22'). Face names are 18px/600, star counts '★3'/'★1' 18px/900, feed times '25m ago' 18px, reminder bylines 18px, feed lines 26px and reminder text 22px. At 1920x1000 the feed lines drop to 22px (index.html:175, max-height:1050px) and everything else stays the same. The CSS matches: tv-face uses fs-sm (index.html:153), .when uses fs-sm (:163), .rem-by uses fs-sm (:172), and the kiosk block design.css:286-289 starts at --fs-sm. The date inherits .ds .hero-kicker fs-xs (design.css:417). Visual-angle recomputation: a 55-inch 1080p set has a pixel pitch of 0.0634 cm, so 18px = 1.14 cm at 300 cm, which equals 0.152 cm at 40 cm = 7.9 iPad CSS px (0.01924 cm each). On a 65-inch set it is 9.35 px, and 12px becomes 5.3 px. All match the item.
s1.rationale: The TV is a primary device. The stars the kids look for, the names and 'who prayed' are information text that works out to about 8 px at arm's length, well below the iPad's own floor, so reading is measurably hampered. That meets the visual-item bar for medium. It is not high: the avatars and emoji still identify people, and the effect depends on the unknown set size and viewing distance, which the item states honestly.

s2.method: I read the kiosk token block and the TV board CSS, and viewed the full-size 1920x1080 screenshot board-typical-tv-light.png myself. I recomputed the 3 m TV to 40 cm iPad equivalence from first principles (a 55-inch 16:9 panel is 1217.6 mm wide, so 0.634 mm per px; an iPad at 132 CSS px per inch is 0.1924 mm per px) and compared it with remeasure-live-tv-board.json.
s2.observed: The kiosk block (design.css:286-289) sets --fs-sm:18px and leaves --fs-xs at 12px (design.css:22). .tv-face uses --fs-sm (index.html:153), which puts face names and star counts ('Ezra ★3', via .tv-face b) at 18 px. .tv-lines .when uses --fs-sm (:163), for 18 px times. .tv-rem .rem-by uses --fs-sm (:172), for 18 px bylines. The date is .hero-kicker at var(--fs-xs) (design.css:417) with only a colour override for the TV (index.html:141), so 12 px uppercase. Under max-height:1050px, feed lines drop from --fs-lg 26 to --fs-md 22 (:175). The evidence gives 18/600 names, 18/900 stars, 18/400 times and bylines, 12/700 date, 26 lines and 22 reminders, the same in System and Midnight. My recomputation: 18 x 0.634 x 400 / (3000 x 0.1924) = 7.9 px on a 55-inch set (9.35 px on a 65-inch), 12 px becomes 5.3 px and 26 px becomes 11.4 px, all matching remeasure-tvmath.json. In the screenshot, the 'TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 22' date is visibly tiny beside the 172 px clock, and the star counts are small captions under 72 px avatars.
s2.rationale: The TV is one of the listed primary devices. Star counts and 'who prayed' are exactly what kids and parents look for from across the room, and at a 7.9 px iPad-equivalent on a 55-inch set, reading them is measurably hampered. Avatars partly carry identity, but not the star numbers or times. The workaround is walking up to the set. That fits 'medium: … measurably hampers reading … on a primary device'. It does not reach high: the board is ambient, and nothing is broken or wrong.
s2.correction: Small detail: 'names … are 18 px' applies to the face captions under avatars. The names in the 'Around the house' feed lines (.who) inherit the line size, 26 px (22 px under 1050 px height).

s1.method: Counted <symbol> and <use href="#…"> in every shipped HTML file, grepped the apps for any reference to icons/*.svg, and tallied the declared stroke-width values per file. Read the cited Kids-card and F260 lines, and checked the family table (Table ICON-1) against the headline count. Viewed the F260 milestones screenshot.
s1.observed: index.html has 21 <symbol> and 30 <use>. f260.html has 11 <symbol> and 10 <use>. Every other app has 0/0, and no app references icons/*.svg, so no app uses the shell's set. Declared strokes: Dollywood 0.7-9 (mostly 2, 2.4, 2.6, 3), F260 2/2.5/2.6 (CHECK on a 20 grid at 2.6, f260.html:1183), Prayer 1.75-2.4, Verses 1.75-2.25, Kid Verse 1.75-2.2. The shell uses 1.75 through design.css. rollup.json gives the shell 1.02-3.85 px rendered across 11 sizes. The Kids card puts ${ICON_STAR} in its head beside text '★${k.stars}' chips (index.html:913-915). F260 draws Previous/Next week as a text −/+ (f260.html:617-620) but as chevron SVGs in the reading bar (:692-694). The milestones screenshot shows colour emoji, ✎/♥ glyphs, stroked printer and gear icons, text − and +, CSS chevrons and SVG ticks together. But Table ICON-1 has 12 rows (F1-F8, G, E, C, A), not eleven, or 10 if the shell's F1-F3 are one recipe as the item itself says.

Still, the rule gives a consistency item medium only when it misleads, hides information, or measurably hampers reading or tapping. Each icon still communicates its meaning in context, the star/star and chevron/± pairs do not mislead, and the contrast and target failures are filed separately. What is left is cosmetic, so low.

s1.method: I read the icon rules in apps/design.css and the Icons section of docs/design.html, counted <symbol> sprites per file, and recomputed the select chevron's contrast against --surface in all five palettes with my own script. There are no icon size or stroke tokens, and the kid/kiosk blocks (:280-289) do not rescale icons. The shell renders 11 sizes, 14-53 px; F260 renders 16-64 px. The shell's stroke range of 1.02-3.85 px is just the fixed 1.75/24 viewBox stroke scaled with size (14 px gives 1.02, 53 px gives 3.86), so it is proportional, not erratic. The real harms it mentions (ink on a tint, raw person colours in dark, the broken .duo fill) are filed separately (P4-ICON-01/-02/-03, P4-DARK-01). The chevron passes 3:1 in every palette, and the 26 px kid tab icons sit inside kid-size targets. Under the feature-gap rule this is nice to have, so low, not medium.
s1.correction: Minor points only. The style guide has three #i-plus copies on hex --tint tiles plus one bare icon-lg, not four each on a hex tint. F260 carries its own 11-symbol sprite, so index.html is not the only inline sprite; what is true is that no shared, loadable sprite exists. The 1.02-3.85 px stroke range is the single 1.75 stroke scaled with icon size, not an inconsistent stroke setting.

s1.method: I wrote my own parser and WCAG/OKLCH calculator for every token block in apps/design.css (audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/GAP-DARK-1/s1-colour.mjs) and recomputed the soft fills, accent-soft and inks against --surface. I then traced each of the six Phase 3 findings the item attributes to the -soft tokens back to the CSS that paints them. I viewed the cited Midnight Larder, Forest Tally and dark Kid-mode Prayer captures.
s1.observed: The token numbers reproduce exactly. Midnight -soft against #241E19: mocha 1.10, gold 1.08, olive 1.07, teal 1.02, terra 1.01, slate 1.11. Forest: 1.02-1.10. Midnight accent-soft: 1.09-1.22 for the seven household people. Hearth soft fills: 1.16-1.21 at C 0.014-0.037. Inks on their fills: 8.9-10.4:1. The claim that one token choice explains six findings does not hold for four of them. (1) Prayer's kid fills are --accent-deep versus --olive (prayer.html:421,427), not a -soft token. (2) Tally's discs are glass, var(--glass-strong) (tally.html:41-48,73-76,96-101); tally.html uses no -soft token. (3) Kid Verse's 'dots 1.14' and 'badge discs 1.15' are --surface-2 against --surface (Midnight 1.14, Forest 1.16; kidverse.html:66,83). An earned day shows a gold star glyph (gold on gold-soft 7.79:1), and an earned badge gets a solid gold disc. (4) F260 goes through --sunk, as the item itself admits. Where -soft really is the fill (Larder status chips, Verses Not yet/Almost buttons, the shell stars card), the state is also carried by a text label in glowing ink. In the Midnight Larder capture, 'Use it up', 'Aging' and 'Fresh' each also have a coloured left rail, a coloured freshness bar and a section heading. Nothing disappears.
s1.rationale: The dark soft fills are indeed near-invisible tints, but they sit behind redundant high-contrast cues everywhere I traced them. Nothing is hidden or misleading, and no tap is hampered. The findings where a state really is weak for kids (Prayer's kid button, Kid Verse's unearned discs, Tally's discs) are caused by other tokens and are filed on their own. That leaves an aesthetic 'muddy, not glowing' departure from the house style. Under the visual rule (medium needs a real effect on use) this is low.
s1.correction: The measured token contrasts are right, but the causal claim is wrong. The -soft tokens do not explain VIS-TALLY-1 (glass discs), VIS-KIDVERSE-3 (the 1.14/1.15 figures are surface-2 against surface), the Prayer kid fills (accent-deep against olive) or VIS-F260-2 (--sunk). 'Every soft-filled state vanishes' and 'for pre-readers the fill is the state cue' are overstated: the Larder and Verses states carry labelled ink at 8.9-10.4:1, and Kid Verse's earned days carry a gold star.

s2.method: I parsed every theme block in apps/design.css and computed each -soft token's contrast against --surface, plus --accent-soft for the 7 household colours (s2-soft.mjs). I sampled rendered pixels in the full-size Midnight captures of Verses and Larder (s2-pixels.mjs). I read the CSS behind each cited Phase 3 finding (leftovers.html:139-141, verses.html:56-58, kidverse.html:66-68/277, prayer.html:421-427) and viewed the dark screenshots.
s2.observed: The token maths reproduces the report. In Midnight the soft fills measure mocha 1.10, gold 1.08, olive 1.07, teal 1.02, terra 1.01 and slate 1.11 against the card; Forest runs 1.02-1.10; household --accent-soft is 1.09-1.22 in both. The inks on their fills are 8.9-10.4:1. The rendered pixels agree: Verses Not yet 1.02 and Almost 1.09 against the card, Larder Aging 1.08 and Fresh 1.07 against the row. The light themes are also low: Hearth 1.16-1.21, Parchment 1.14-1.21, Frost 1.15-1.21, so the dark-only drop is only about 0.1. In every cited case the state is still carried elsewhere. Larder chips are text labels, and each row also has a coloured left rail, a freshness bar and a section heading. The Verses buttons have an icon and a text label. On a Kid Verse day that is 'on', a gold star glyph replaces the weekday letter. Prayer's kid prayed and unprayed buttons are --accent-deep against --olive, which are solid fills, not -soft tokens.
s2.rationale: This is a visual/token gap. The fill shape fades, but no information is hidden or misleading, because the ink labels and glyphs carry every state at 8.9-10.4:1 and WCAG 1.4.11 does not require a boundary on a labelled button. That falls short of the medium bar ('misleads, hides information, or measurably hampers reading or tapping'). It is a real but cosmetic loss on the Kitchen iPad each evening under System, so low.
s2.correction: "Every soft-filled state goes muddy or vanishes" is true only of the fill shape. The state itself survives in ink text or icons in every cited case. "For pre-readers the fill is the state cue" is wrong for Kid Verse: an earned day shows a gold star glyph (kidverse.html:68,277). Prayer's kid prayed/unprayed pair is --accent-deep against --olive (prayer.html:421,427), not a -soft token, so this token choice does not explain it. Household --accent-soft is 1.09-1.22 (1.08 only with the extra swatches). The light themes sit at 1.14-1.21 too, well under the item's own 1.4 target, so the dark-specific part is small.

s1.method: I recomputed OKLCH, the derived accent-soft and accent-deep, and CIEDE2000 for all 21 household pairs from worker/seed.sql and the design.css token formulas with my own code. I also ran my own Machado-2009 colour-blindness simulation (s1-cvd.mjs). I then traced where person colours are painted, to check whether any screen tells people apart by colour alone.
s1.observed: Every number reproduces. The seven household colours sit at L 0.436-0.648, C 0.058-0.135 (0.42 with the TV). Hearth accent-soft has C 0.004-0.026, and Eli's is #E6E6E9 at C 0.004. Dark accent-deep has C 0.031-0.086: Elizabeth #BBA997 0.033, David #8E9F8E 0.031. Six of the 21 Hearth accent-soft pairs are under ΔE00 5: David/Mea 2.44, Mae/Elizabeth 4.10. The picker offers ten swatches (index.html:449). Under colour-blindness, deuteranopia puts Elizabeth/Mea at 2.14 and protanopia puts Mae/Elizabeth at 4.79. However, the raw colours are all at least ΔE00 15.4 apart under normal vision. The 14% accent-soft is the signed-in person's own UI tint, so only one person's appears on a screen. Wherever several people's colours appear, they come with a face or a name: hub.avatarHtml paints the emoji or photo on a 30-55% mix with a 5 px raw-colour ring (design.css:491-494); the feed prints the name; the park map puts the emoji on the marker. So hue alone never identifies a person, as the house rule requires.
s1.rationale: The low chroma and the near-grey soft fills are a real aesthetic departure from the 'vibrant pastel' house style. But the 'people run together as fills' collision is measured on a derived fill that is never used to tell people apart, and the raw colours that are are always paired with an emoji, photo or name. Nothing misleads, hides information or hampers tapping, and the dark accent-deep inks stay legible. Under the visual rule this is low.
s1.correction: 'As fills, people run together' is true only of the 14% accent-soft, which is never shown side by side for different people. The person marks that do appear together use the raw colour (at least ΔE00 15.4 apart) plus an emoji or photo, so the collisions (including the colour-blind ones on the raw colours) cause no misidentification. 'Neither distinct enough' is overstated for the raw colours under normal vision.

s2.method: With my own colour script (s2-colour.mjs + s2-accent.mjs: OKLCH, CIEDE2000, color-mix in srgb, Vienot CVD) I recomputed the OKLCH of the seed colours, the 14% --accent-soft in every theme, the dark --accent-deep, and all 21 household pairs. I compared the results with tokens.json. I also checked where people's colours appear side by side (hub.avatarHtml, the .avatar and .person-chip CSS) and viewed the Hearth Home capture.
s2.observed: The seed colours sit at OKLCH L 0.436-0.648 (0.421 with the TV). In Hearth, --accent-soft is C 0.004-0.026, and Eli's is #E6E6E9 at C 0.004, which matches the report. The dark --accent-deep is C 0.031-0.086: Elizabeth #BBA997 at 0.033, David #8E9F8E at 0.031. On the Home capture, Eli's accent-soft buttons ('Open F260') render visibly grey. My CIEDE2000 of the Hearth soft fills puts 5 of 21 pairs under 5: David/Mea 2.78, Elizabeth/David 4.02, Kiara/Elizabeth 4.13, Mae/Elizabeth 4.50, Ezra/Mea 4.80. Ezra/David is just over at 5.12. Under CVD I found deutan Elizabeth/Mea 1.86 and protan Mae/Elizabeth 4.28. As raw colours with normal vision, all 21 pairs are at or above ΔE00 15.4. The .person-chip class, the one component that paints another person's 14% fill, is used nowhere in index.html or apps/. Avatars use a 30-55% mix plus a raw-colour ring, and they carry an emoji or photo; names sit beside them (e.g. the Home Kids card).
s2.rationale: The claims are mostly true, but the effect is aesthetic, a deviation from the house pastel style. The soft fill is almost always the signed-in person's own accent, shown alone. Where several people appear together, they are told apart by name, emoji or photo and by the raw-colour ring, and those rings are all at ΔE00 15.4 or more. The deep ink on soft reads at 7:1 or better. Nothing misleads or hides information, so this is low under the visual rule. The grey soft buttons looking slightly disabled is the most concrete cost, and it is cosmetic.
s2.correction: "6/21 household pairs under ΔE00 5" is borderline: an independent CIEDE2000 gives 5/21 (David/Mea 2.78, not 2.43; Mae/Elizabeth 4.50, not 4.1), with Ezra/David at 5.12. "As fills, people run together" overstates the exposure. No shipped component paints two people's 14% soft fills side by side (.person-chip is unused), and avatars use a stronger mix, a raw ring and an emoji or photo.

s1.method: I wrote my own script (audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/VIS-COLOR-1/s1-recompute.mjs). It parses the tokens straight from apps/design.css and apps.json and recomputes OKLCH chroma and hue, the tile gradient stops, icon-to-tile contrast, card/page and well/page ratios and bar-to-track contrast for all five palettes. It does not reuse the phase-4 tools. I also checked the cited lines and looked at the full-size shell screenshots (apps and home, iPad portrait, light and dark).
s1.observed: Soft-fill chroma: Hearth 0.014-0.037, Parchment 0.008-0.070, Frost 0.011-0.032, Midnight 0.021-0.032, Forest 0.012-0.031. The house pastels are 0.057-0.093, so the fills sit at about a third of house chroma, as claimed. Parchment gold-soft at 0.070 is the only exception. Six token families with hues 38-274 across palettes (Hearth 39-271). There is no pink or lavender family, and slate sits at about 271°, so Sky and Periwinkle both map to it. The tile gradient is 22% to 8% tint over --surface (design.css:606-608), with stop chroma mostly 0.002-0.056. The hero is at :412, the wash at :70-71 (accent 10% plus gold 6% in Hearth) and the bar start (75% tint plus white) at :534, all confirmed. Dark card/page is 1.099 in Midnight and 1.116 in Forest, against iOS 1.234. The dark well is darker than the page at 1.037/1.042. The Hearth page is L 0.963, C 0.011, H 77, and iOS #F2F2F7 is L 0.963, C 0.007, H 286. Parchment's page is L 0.89, C 0.039. Tile icon (raw app colour) against the two stops: Kid Verse in light is 2.57/2.98 in Hearth, 2.21/2.50 in Parchment and 2.54/2.94 in Frost. In dark the Larder is 1.83-2.04 and F260 2.12-2.42. The problem is also broader in dark: Dollywood is 2.24-2.56 and the park map 2.49-2.93, while Prayer, Tally, Verses and Timer drop under 3 against the 22% stop. Bar start against track (light only) is 1.83-2.98. Gold, the warn fridge bar, is the lowest (1.93 in Hearth, 1.83 in Parchment), and gold's full-tint end is 2.69 in Hearth. In dark the bars are 9.3-11.5:1. The only .bar users on design.css are the fridge freshness bars (Home and the Larder), and each has a days count as text beside it. In the screenshots every tile icon is recognisable and has a text label, the dark cards are visibly separated (edge ring plus the 1.10 step), and the fridge bars are legible.
s1.rationale: The item describes a gap between the shipped palette and the house style: fill chroma, missing hue families, the tile gradient direction and the iOS neutrals. None of that misleads, hides information or measurably hampers reading or tapping. The rule says that for a visual item, medium needs a real effect on use (text under AA, or targets under 44 px in a daily flow); otherwise it is low. The parts that touch legibility are non-text graphics, and each has a redundant text channel: tile icons have the app name under them, and fridge bars have the '8d' day count. Dark cards stay distinguishable in the iPad screenshots. Text-contrast failures from raw accents are filed separately (P4-COLOR-02/03, P2-VIS-06). The exposure is every palette and every device, but the effect is cosmetic, so it rates low, not medium.
s1.correction: The rating is inflated: the item shows no effect on use beyond cosmetic, so it is low, not medium. The bar figure '2.27-2.99' covers only the start stop in the light palettes. Recomputed from tokens it is 1.83-2.98, with gold (the warn fridge bar) lowest at 1.83-1.93. In dark the bars are 9-11:1, not failing. The dark tile-icon problem goes beyond 'the Larder's and F260's (1.95-2.33)': the Larder is 1.83-2.04, F260 2.12-2.42, and Dollywood (2.24-2.56) and the park map (2.49-2.93) also fail across both stops. The Kid Verse light range recomputes as 2.21-2.98 across the stops, not 2.39-2.81. 'Sit at the pastels' lightness (L 0.87-0.94)' applies to the light palettes only, since the dark soft fills are deep tints. The family hue span is 38-274 across palettes, a trivial difference.

s2.method: I wrote audits/tools/phase5/ux-verify/VIS-COLOR-1/s2-recompute.mjs. It parses every palette's hex values straight from apps/design.css and recomputes OKLCH, WCAG contrast and the color-mix tile stops and bar stops, without reading the investigator's palette.json. I compared the results with the house pastels in audits/HUB-AUDIT-PROMPT.md:57-64 and with the rendered non-text measurements. I also viewed the full-size iPad Apps screenshots in light and dark, and checked what text sits next to each sub-3:1 graphic.
s2.observed: Soft fills: C 0.014-0.037 in Hearth, 0.008-0.070 in Parchment (gold-soft is the 0.070), 0.011-0.032 in Frost, 0.021-0.032 in Midnight and 0.012-0.031 in Forest. Light-palette soft L is 0.871-0.942. The eight house pastels are C 0.057-0.093 at L 0.876-0.953. Hearth's median soft C is about 0.025 against a house median of about 0.066, so 'about a third' is fair. --accent-soft for the ten swatches is C 0.004-0.047 (the report says the same). Ink on every soft fill is 5.37-10.35:1, so the low-chroma fills cause no text-contrast failure. Tile icon ink on its tile stops: Kid Verse 2.21-2.98 across the three light palettes (the rendered measure is 2.39-2.81). Larder in dark is 1.83-2.04 (rendered minimum 1.95) and F260 in dark is 2.12-2.43 (rendered 2.28-2.33). All three are under 3:1, but every tile carries its app name as text, and the dim icons are still visible in apps-typical-ipad-portrait-dark.png. The .bar fill against its track in light runs 1.83-3.98 from the start to the end of the gradient (the report says 2.27-2.99); in dark it is 7.2-11.4. The Home fridge bars sit under a text line (.fl, index.html:120) with the item name and age. Dark card against page is 1.10 in Midnight and 1.12 in Forest, against 1.23 for iOS; the dark well against the page is 1.04. Cards also have a line-soft border, which shows in the screenshot. The six token hue families span H 37.9-273.8. Bubblegum (354) and Lavender (303) have no token family, and Sky (252) and Periwinkle (278) both land on slate (271). However, the profile swatch list includes plum #8C4F7A (H 339). App colours include purple #7A4FA3 (H 306) and blue #1F6FB2 (H 249).
s2.rationale: The substance holds: the shipped palette is low-chroma earth tones, not the house pastels, and the dark palettes have little card lift. Under the severity rule, a visual item is medium only if it misleads, hides information, or measurably hampers reading or tapping. None of that is shown here. Every text-on-fill pair passes AA with margin. The sub-3:1 graphics (tile icons, freshness bars) all repeat information that is already on screen as text. Dark cards are still separated by their borders. So this is a style deviation from the constitution's colour rule with at most a minor, cosmetic effect on use, which is low. Exposure is every screen on every device, and I weighed that, but breadth alone does not raise the rating.
s2.correction: (1) The six families span H about 38-274, not 42-274 (Hearth terra is 39.4 and Frost terra 37.9). (2) 'In all five palettes' is correct for chroma, but the lightness match (L 0.87-0.94) applies only to the three light palettes; the dark soft fills sit at L 0.24-0.28. (3) 'Two house hues missing' is true of the token families used for chips and semantics, but not of the profile swatches: plum #8C4F7A is at H 339. The app colours also already carry a purple (306) and a blue (249). (4) The bar-against-track range is wider than stated in light (1.83-3.98 along the gradient) and is 7-11:1 in dark, so 'the bars read 2.27-2.99' holds only for mid-gradient samples in light. (5) The sub-3:1 icons and bars are all paired with a visible text label, so they hide no information. The medium rating is therefore inflated; low is right.
